title: First solids of the Solar System condense
text: Calcium-aluminium-rich inclusions (CAIs), the oldest dated Solar System solids, form in the disk around the young Sun. Their age is the conventional 'time zero' of the Solar System.

title: First protoplanets: the parent bodies of iron meteorites
text: Within a few hundred thousand years of the first solids, bodies large enough to melt have accreted and begin separating metal cores. Iron meteorites are fragments of those cores.

title: Jupiter's core forms: the oldest planet
text: Isotopes in meteorites show Jupiter's solid core reached about 20 Earth masses within a million years, and about 50 by 3–4 million years. Its gravity split the disk into inner and outer reservoirs, which may explain why the Solar System has no super-Earths.

title: Mars reaches half its present size
text: Hafnium–tungsten dating of Martian meteorites shows Mars grew to about half its size within roughly 2 million years. It is a stranded planetary embryo that never merged into a larger planet.

title: A molten protoplanet freezes: the parent body of the HED meteorites
text: A magma ocean on the parent body of the howardite–eucrite–diogenite meteorites begins crystallizing within about 0.6 million years of the first solids and is nearly solid 2–3 million years later. That parent body is usually identified as Vesta, but this study argued it must be smaller; debated.

title: The Sun's gas disk disperses
text: Angrite meteorites that crystallized 4,563.5 million years ago recorded almost no magnetic field, showing that the gas disk around the young Sun, and the field it carried, had cleared within about 4 million years.

title: Mars has a core, a solidified magma ocean and a first crust
text: Zircons in a Martian meteorite show that Mars had finished accreting, formed its core and crystallized its magma ocean into a primordial crust less than 20 million years after the Solar System began.

title: Earth's iron core separates
text: Hafnium–tungsten dating of meteorites indicates that the cores of the terrestrial planets, Earth's included, formed within about the first 30 million years of the Solar System. Smaller bodies such as Vesta and Mars formed their cores sooner.

title: The Sun leaves the star cluster it was born in
text: Simulations suggest the Sun escaped its birth cluster 20–50 million years after the Solar System formed. Most of the Oort cloud of comets built up afterwards, and part of it may consist of comets captured from other stars.

title: The giant planets shuffle orbits; Neptune herds Pluto
text: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune move to new orbits and scatter the outer disk of icy bodies; Neptune's outward migration can explain Pluto's 3:2 resonance with it. Recent studies put this within about 100 million years of the gas disk clearing (before 4,480 million years ago); the original Nice model placed it some 700 million years after planet formation. Debated.

title: The Moon forms
text: Zircons from Apollo 14 samples indicate the Moon had formed and differentiated by about 4.51 billion years ago, most likely after a giant impact on the proto-Earth.

title: Mars has a magnetic field
text: MAVEN magnetic data show a Martian core dynamo was active about 4.5 billion years ago, early in the planet's history.

title: Oldest dated piece of Mars
text: A zircon grain in the Martian meteorite Northwest Africa 7034 crystallizes 4,476 million years ago, the oldest directly dated material from Mars.

title: A younger Moon? The alternative formation date
text: A model in which the lunar magma ocean crystallized slowly, fitted to the isotopes of lunar rocks, places the Moon's formation at 4.40–4.45 billion years ago, later than the 4.51 billion years given by lunar zircons. Debated.

title: Oldest known piece of Earth: the Jack Hills zircon
text: A detrital zircon crystal from Western Australia records continental-type crust and probably liquid water at the surface.

title: Oldest well-dated lunar crust: anorthosite 60025
text: Ferroan anorthosite 60025, a piece of the Moon's pale highland crust returned by Apollo 16, crystallized 4,360 million years ago by three isotope clocks. Either the lunar magma ocean solidified late or this crust formed some other way; debated.

title: Water on the surface: the first oceans?
text: Oxygen isotopes in 4.3-billion-year-old zircon grains from the Jack Hills, Western Australia, show they grew from magma that had melted crust once altered by liquid water near the surface. A hydrosphere, perhaps oceans, was already in contact with the crust.

title: Hadean crust in Quebec? The Nuvvuagittuq belt
text: Neodymium-142 in rocks of the Nuvvuagittuq greenstone belt suggests they formed about 4.28 billion years ago, which would make them the oldest surviving crust. Others argue for about 3.8 billion years; debated.

title: South Pole–Aitken: the Moon's largest and oldest basin forms
text: Impact-melt norites in soil returned from the lunar far side by Chang'e-6 date the South Pole–Aitken basin, the largest and oldest well-preserved impact structure on the Moon, to 4.25 billion years ago. First sample-based date for the basin.

title: Earliest claimed record of Earth's magnetic field
text: Magnetization in Jack Hills zircons suggests a geodynamo was operating 4.2 billion years ago, only a few hundred million years after Earth formed. A re-analysis argues the magnetization is later and that the field before 3.5 billion years ago remains unknown; debated.

title: LUCA: the last universal common ancestor
text: A molecular-clock study places the last common ancestor of all living things at about 4.2 billion years ago, already a complex prokaryote with an early immune system. The date is uncertain and debated.

title: Continents already exist: zircons older than any rock
text: Four detrital zircon grains from quartzite at Mount Narryer, Western Australia, crystallized 4.1–4.2 billion years ago. Found in 1983 by ion microprobe, they were the first proof that crust existed on Earth before 3.8 billion years ago, long before the oldest surviving rocks. Grains this old later turned up far away too: 4,127 ± 4 million years at Longquan in southern China, and 3.96 billion in Montana's Beartooth Mountains.
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: cathaysia-hadean-zircon (xing2014), beartooth-zircons (mueller1992).

title: Mars's crust stops recording a magnetic field: did its dynamo die?
text: Large impact basins on Mars older than about 4.12 billion years (crater-count model age) hold re-magnetized crust; younger ones are demagnetized, and the switch took under 20 million years. One reading is that the martian dynamo died; others argue that a field persisted and the younger basins simply excavated less magnetic rock.

title: Mineral inclusions in Jack Hills zircons hint at Hadean subduction
text: Mineral inclusions in Jack Hills zircons 4.02–4.19 billion years old show that their magmas formed at about 700 °C and 7 kbar. That implies low heat flow, three to five times below estimates for the Hadean Earth as a whole, as found today only above subduction zones; a sign, contested, that plates were already converging.

title: Possible traces of life in a 4.1-billion-year-old zircon
text: Graphite sealed inside a Jack Hills zircon has a light carbon-isotope signature that may be biological. Debated.

title: ALH84001: the oldest martian igneous rock, and the 1996 'life on Mars' claim
text: The martian meteorite ALH84001 crystallized 4.091 ± 0.030 billion years ago (lutetium–hafnium age), during heavy bombardment and around the time Mars's magnetic field faded. Its magma came from the same deep mantle source that fed much younger shergottite lavas 150–570 million years ago. In 1996 a team argued that carbonate globules, organic molecules and tiny magnetite grains inside it could be fossil remains of martian microbes; they allowed that non-biological origins were possible, and the claim remains disputed.
notes: Life claim from mckay1996 abstract (PAHs, carbonate globules, single-domain magnetite; 'inorganic formation is possible'), added 2026-11-23.

title: Mercury's oldest surviving surface forms
text: Heavy bombardment and volcanism resurface all of Mercury about 4.0–4.1 billion years ago, erasing its earlier history; volcanism ends within 300–400 million years. Ages come from crater counts, since no samples of Mercury exist.

title: Tubes from ancient sea-floor vents: life 3.77–4.28 billion years ago?
text: Tubes and filaments of iron oxide in Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq belt resemble fossils of microbes from hydrothermal vents, between 3.77 and 4.28 billion years old. Both the age and the biological origin are debated.

title: Acasta Gneiss: oldest known intact rocks
text: Granite-like gneisses in northwestern Canada crystallized 4.00–4.03 billion years ago, the oldest dated whole rocks on Earth. First dated in 1989 at 3,962 million years, they were pushed past 4 billion a decade later. They were reheated again and again, near 3.75, 3.6 and 1.7 billion years ago.
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: acasta-gneiss-3962 (bowring1989), acasta-reheated (bowring1999).

title: Life before 3.95 billion years ago? Light carbon in Labrador
text: Graphite in metasediments of the Saglek Block, northern Labrador, is up to 25‰ lighter in carbon-13 than carbonate in the same rocks, which its discoverers read as a trace of life older than 3.95 billion years. Critics say field relations and zircon ages fail to show the sediments are that old; they may be far younger.

title: Nectaris basin forms on the Moon
text: The Nectaris impact basin is dated to 3.92 billion years ago (an alternative reading gives 3.85). Its ejecta defines the start of the Moon's Nectarian period.

title: The Moon has a strong magnetic field
text: Apollo samples record a lunar core dynamo producing surface fields of several tens of microtesla from 4.25 to 3.56 billion years ago.

title: Imbrium basin forms on the Moon
text: The impact that excavated the Imbrium basin is dated between 3.85 and 3.94 billion years ago depending on which Apollo samples are attributed to it; phosphates in Apollo 14 breccias give 3,934 million years.

title: Late Heavy Bombardment: heavy impacts on the Moon and Earth
text: Lunar impact-melt rocks and meteorite shock ages point to elevated impacts between about 4.2–4.0 and 3.5 billion years ago. Whether this was a sharp 'cataclysm' or the tail of a declining bombardment is debated; large impacts on Earth continued to about 2.5–2.0 billion years ago. Rocks from the Moon's far side, returned by Chang'e-6, record an impact 3.87 billion years ago, alongside the great nearside basins.
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: spa-second-impact-3870 (su2025).

title: Akilia, Greenland: the 1996 'earliest life' claim
text: In 1996 isotopically light carbon inside apatite grains from a banded rock on Akilia island was announced as life older than 3.8, possibly 3.85 billion years. The rock is at least 3,825 ± 6 million years old, but critics argued it is altered igneous rock, not sediment, and later found no graphite in the apatite at all.

title: Orientale basin: the Moon's youngest great basin
text: Crater counts on its ejecta give an age of about 3.80 billion years for Orientale, the youngest and best-preserved multi-ring basin on the Moon; earlier counts ranged from 3.68 to 3.8 billion years.

title: Oldest known eroded sediments settle in a Greenland fore-arc
text: The inner panels of the Isua belt formed 3.72–3.69 billion years ago. Their turbidites and muds, the oldest known detrital sediments, were eroded from basalt and tonalite and laid down over chemical sediments on boninite-like lava. One team reads this as a fore-arc basin above a young subduction zone; whether plate tectonics ran this early is disputed.

title: Rivers and lakes fill Gale crater on Mars
text: Layered sediment builds the great mound inside Gale crater 3.8–3.6 billion years ago. Streams, deltas and lakes deposit at least 75 metres of sediment in it, lasting intermittently for thousands to millions of years: evidence of a wetter early Mars, explored by the Curiosity rover.

title: Possible oldest record of Earth's magnetic field, in Isua iron formation
text: Banded iron formation in northeast Isua, Greenland, may hold a magnetization acquired 3.7 billion years ago, recording a field stronger than 15 µT; a fold test using folding 3.6 billion years ago supports it. A field this weak may have let more of the atmosphere escape.

title: Isua 'stromatolites': oldest fossils, or folded rock?
text: Cone-shaped structures in 3.7-billion-year-old rocks of Greenland were described as microbial stromatolites; a re-examination concluded they are deformed rock. Debated.

title: Mars still has a global magnetic field
text: Magnetized lava flows at Lucus Planum show a Martian core dynamo was active 3.7 billion years ago, as it was 4.5 billion years ago. The giant basins formed in between are unmagnetized, so when and how the field died is debated.

title: Two Greenland terranes collide: crust thickens as in a modern collision
text: Near Isua in southwest Greenland, a block of crust about 3.7 billion years old was pushed against one about 3.8 billion years old between 3.68 and 3.66 billion years ago. A rare high-pressure granulite of about 3.66 billion years shows the crust was thickened. The authors see convergent plate boundaries; others argue the early Archean mantle was too hot for rigid plates (debated). The thickened crust was then heated, stretched and invaded by granites until 3.60 billion years ago (the Isukasian orogeny).
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: isukasian-orogeny (nutman2013).

title: Eswatini's oldest rocks: new continent made by remelting older crust
text: The oldest grey gneisses of the Ancient Gneiss Complex in Eswatini (Swaziland) formed 3.66 billion years ago by remelting older crust, perhaps Late Hadean: their hafnium model ages are 3.77 to 4.08 billion years. New crust from the mantle followed between 3.54 and 3.32 billion years ago.

title: An ocean on Mars? The Deuteronilus contact
text: A sharp boundary traced for thousands of kilometres across Mars's northern plains has surfaces with crater-count ages near 3.6 billion years. Its shape fits neither lava nor ice, and the authors read it as the shore of a water or mud ocean (debated).
notes: Age and claim from a web-search summary of the abstract; abstract not retrievable (Elsevier 403). See verification-backlog.md.

title: East Pilbara: granite domes rise through sinking lavas
text: In Western Australia's East Pilbara, granitoids intruded from about 3.60 to 3.46 billion years ago and rose through denser lavas above them in gravitational overturns; the last ended about 3.413 billion years ago. The crust grew in cycles of about 100 million years before it was rigid enough for plate-like behaviour.

title: Oldest known impact debris on Earth
text: Identically dated spherule layers in the Pilbara (Australia) and Kaapvaal (South Africa) cratons form a single global fallout layer from a large impact 3.47 billion years ago, with tsunami deposits beneath.
notes: 3.47 Ga from memory; check against the paper. 'Close together' interpretation to check too.

title: Apex chert microfossils
text: Carbon isotopes measured in individual filaments from the 3.465-billion-year-old Apex chert of Australia match different microbial groups, supporting them as the oldest known microfossils. Debated.

title: Methane-making microbes
text: Methane with a biological isotope signature, trapped in 3.46-billion-year-old fluid inclusions in Australia, is the oldest evidence for methanogenesis.

title: Strelley Pool: a 3.43-billion-year-old microbial reef
text: Seven kinds of stromatolites spread across an ancient coastal platform in Western Australia; their variety and setting point to a reef built by microbes.

art.caption: A stromatolite cut open: layer upon layer of sediment trapped and bound by microbial mats. Strelley Pool preserves seven kinds of these structures.

title: Earth's magnetic shield is in place
text: Rocks from South Africa's Kaapvaal craton record a geodynamo 3.45–3.4 billion years ago. With the stronger solar wind of the young Sun, the magnetosphere reached only about half its present distance.

title: Hot tub or temperate sea? How warm the Archean ocean was
text: Hot view: oxygen and silicon isotopes in Barberton cherts imply 55 to 85 °C seawater, and proteins rebuilt from ancient gene sequences work best when hot. Temperate view: seawater's own isotope mix has drifted and later fluids altered the cherts; pairing oxygen with hydrogen isotopes in the 3.42-billion-year-old Buck Reef Chert gives 40 °C or less. Debated.

title: Buck Reef Chert: sunlit microbial mats that made no oxygen
text: In the Buck Reef Chert of South Africa's Barberton belt, carbon-rich microbial mats grew only in shallow, sunlit, wave-washed water, so they were almost certainly photosynthetic. No oxidized minerals accompany them: the microbes probably used hydrogen rather than water to fix carbon, and so released no oxygen into a sea and sky that had none.

title: Komatiites: the hottest lavas Earth has made
text: Named for the Komati River in Barberton, komatiite lavas erupted at about 1,600 °C, some 400 °C hotter than any lava today, a sign of the hot Archean mantle. Almost as runny as water, they rushed out in turbulent floods at metres per second, melting channels into the ground. Cooling from the top, each flow grew long blade-like olivine crystals called spinifex over a base of settled olivine.

art.caption: Cross-section of a komatiite flow, a few metres thick (schematic). Olivine blades of spinifex grew down from the chilled, cracked top; olivine crystals that sank collected below.

notes: Span 3.5–3.3 Ga = approximate range of Barberton (Onverwacht Group) komatiite volcanism; check against arndt2008. Speed: Huppert et al. turbulent flow, metres per second.

title: Today's bacteria and archaea start to branch out
text: Molecular clocks place the common ancestors of all living bacteria and of all living archaea after 3.4 billion years ago, long after LUCA. The oldest fossil traces of life therefore belong to extinct early branches of these lineages.

title: Vaalbara: were South Africa and Australia one landmass?
text: The Kaapvaal (South Africa) and Pilbara (Australia) cratons hold almost all surviving crust from 3.6–2.7 billion years ago, and their rock records match, down to debris from the same 3.47-billion-year-old impact. Joined as Vaalbara, they may form Earth's oldest continent: assembled by 3.1 billion years ago, possibly 3.6, and split by 2.1. Debated; the firmest magnetic evidence is younger.

art.caption: Today the Kaapvaal (South Africa) and Pilbara (Western Australia) cratons lie about 8,900 km apart across the Indian Ocean. Vaalbara would have joined them.

notes: t = midpoint of assembly estimate (by 3.1 Ga, possibly 3.6 Ga) per zegers1998 abstract.

title: Josefsdal Chert: a mixed microbial community at warm seeps
text: Shallow coastal sediments in Barberton's Josefsdal Chert preserve a whole community: photosynthetic mats spread over the surface while chemical-eating microbes lived on volcanic grains and fed on hydrothermal fluids seeping up through the same sediment. Like the older Buck Reef mats, they thrived without oxygen.

title: Giant impacts boil the ocean surface
text: Spherule beds record at least 16 major Archean impacts by bodies over 10 km across. In South Africa's Barberton belt, giants of 3.29 and 3.23 billion years ago heated the atmosphere, boiled the ocean surface and evaporated tens of metres to perhaps 100 m of seawater. Another, S2, about 3.26 billion years ago, raised a tsunami and mixed iron-rich deep water upward; microbial life recovered quickly.
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: archean-impact-s2 (drabon2024).

title: Life on land: microbial mats along Moodies rivers
text: Fossil microbial mats drape river gravels of the Moodies Group, South Africa: the oldest direct evidence of life on land. Their carbon and nitrogen isotopes differ from those of mats in nearby tidal flats, so land communities already cycled nutrients their own way. Shales of the same age hold unusually large organic-walled microfossils that survive tests for a non-biological origin.
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: moodies-microfossils (javaux2010).

title: Microbes learn to fix nitrogen
text: Nitrogen isotopes in 3.2-billion-year-old rocks show molybdenum-based biological nitrogen fixation, making nitrogen from the air available to life.

title: The Pilbara becomes one of the first stable continents
text: Three bursts of mantle-plume volcanism between 3.53 and 3.24 billion years ago left the East Pilbara (Western Australia) on a thick, drained mantle root. By about 3.2 billion years ago it was a buoyant continent that could not be subducted, and its margins were stretched and rifted. Between 3,070 and 3,050 million years ago three younger slices of crust, the West Pilbara terranes, were pushed onto it.

art.caption: Pilbara craton today. The old East Pilbara core lies around Marble Bar; the younger West Pilbara terranes, around Karratha, joined it about 3.07 billion years ago.

notes: Merged 2026-11-23: prinsep-orogeny (vankranendonk2007, kiyokawa2019) with its map; cleaverville-iron-formation cut.

title: The faint young Sun paradox
text: The young Sun shines about 25% dimmer than today; with today's air, Earth would be frozen for its first 2 billion years. Yet Archean rocks show liquid water and life. Extra greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide or methane are the usual answer, but none fits all the evidence and the puzzle is unsolved.

title: Whundo lavas: early subduction, or something stranger?
text: In the Pilbara, a 10-km-thick pile of 3.12-billion-year-old lavas, the Whundo Group, has the chemistry of a modern oceanic island arc, down to boninites, a rare lava of subduction zones. Many read it as early subduction. A 2026 study proposes 'dripduction' instead: short-lived sinking of wet lithosphere, without lasting plate boundaries.

title: Kaapvaal becomes a stable continent, and soon starts to rift
text: After about 3.2 billion years ago the eastern Kaapvaal (South Africa) stopped growing by new melt from the mantle. Its granites of about 3.1 billion years ago formed by remelting older crust, a sign that the block had become a stable craton. By 3,074 ± 5 million years ago it was already being pulled apart: more than 2 km of lavas and ash of the Dominion Group erupted on land in a rift inside the craton, the oldest known, but the rift failed.

art.caption: Kaapvaal craton today. The Barberton greenstone belt is part of the craton's oldest core; the Dominion Group rift lavas lie about 450 km to the west.

notes: Merged 2026-11-23: dominion-group-volcanism (agangi2020) with its map.

title: Archaean genetic expansion: a burst of new gene families
text: Mapping the histories of 3,983 gene families onto geological time suggests that a short burst of innovation, while bacterial lineages rapidly diversified, created 27% of today's major gene families. Many of the new genes run electron-transport and respiratory chains; later genes increasingly use oxygen. The window, roughly 3.33–2.85 billion years ago, rests on molecular-clock dating.
notes: Abstract confirms 3,983 families, 27%, electron transport/respiration, later O2 use; the 3.33-2.85 Ga window is from the paper body, not checked (green OA copy hdl.handle.net/1721.1/61263 refused automated download).

title: Maniitsoq: Earth's oldest impact structure, or not?
text: In 2012 a structure around Maniitsoq, West Greenland, was proposed as the scar of a giant impact about 3 billion years ago, which would make it Earth's oldest known impact structure; zircons reset 3,000.9 ± 1.9 million years ago gave its minimum age. A 2021 survey of 5,587 zircons found no impact signs: the rocks, including norites intruded 3,013–3,001 million years ago, have ordinary explanations.

art.caption: Maniitsoq, West Greenland, today. The proposed impact structure lay in this region; a 2021 study found no evidence of an impact.

title: First whiffs of oxygen
text: Chromium isotopes in South African soils suggest small amounts of oxygen in the air about 3 billion years ago, 600 million years before the Great Oxidation Event. Debated.

title: Plate tectonics gets going
text: The chemistry of ancient sediments shows Earth's upper crust changing from mostly basaltic to granitic around 3 billion years ago, read as the onset of plate tectonics. Diamonds agree: inclusions of recycled oceanic crust (eclogite) appear only after 3.0 billion years ago, and crustal growth slows at the same time. When plate tectonics began is one of geology's most debated questions.

title: Oxygen-producing photosynthesis already at work?
text: Manganese chemistry in 2.95-billion-year-old rocks suggests oxygenic photosynthesis was operating half a billion years before the Great Oxidation Event. Debated.

title: Earth's oldest known glaciation
text: Mudstones of the Mozaan Group in South Africa's Pongola Supergroup hold striated, faceted boulders and stones dropped from floating ice, the oldest reported evidence of glaciers. The rocks barely weathered, as expected of ground-up glacial debris.
notes: Abstract: Mozaan Group ~2.9 Ga, striated and faceted clasts, ice-rafted debris, low CIA. t_err is a rounding allowance for '~2.9 Ga'; Pongola Supergroup spans ~2.98-2.87 Ga.

title: Witwatersrand gold settles in Archean rivers
text: Rivers wash grains of gold, uraninite and pyrite, some eroded from rocks 3.05 billion years old, into gravels of the Witwatersrand basin, South Africa. Mined since 1886, these reefs have given more than a third of the world's gold, about 48,000 tonnes.
notes: Range: Witwatersrand sedimentation onset 2.97 Ga (minter2006) to sills intruding it at 2.79 Ga (gumsley2020); t = midpoint. Detrital pyrite/uraninite as placers (minter2006 abstract, title 'in an Archean atmosphere'). Production figure from phillips2000 abstract (to 2000).

title: Volcanoes on the Moon mostly fall silent
text: Radioisotope ages of lunar basalts show that most volcanic eruptions on the Moon had ended by about 2.9 to 2.8 billion years ago. Basalt brought back by China's Chang'e-5 mission later showed that some eruptions continued until 2.03 billion years ago.
notes: li2021 abstract: 'most lunar basaltic magmatism ceased by around 2.9-2.8 Ga'; Chang'e-5 Pb-Pb age 2,030 ± 4 Ma.

title: Ventersdorp flood basalts begin, sealing in the Witwatersrand gold
text: Floods of basalt lava spread over South Africa's Kaapvaal craton, the first pulse of the Ventersdorp large igneous province. Their feeder sills, dated to 2,789 ± 4 and 2,787 ± 2 million years, cut the gold-bearing Witwatersrand rocks, so the gold is at least this old.
notes: U-Pb ID-TIMS baddeleyite ages on mafic sills interpreted as feeders to Klipriviersberg Group flood basalts. Platberg pulse 2729/2724 Ma (same paper) not added (low priority).

title: A global flare of volcanism stretches the Zimbabwe craton
text: Around 2.75 billion years ago a worldwide surge of magma from the mantle pulled the young Zimbabwe craton apart. The crust sank and several kilometres of submarine basalt piled up in the Belingwe greenstone belt.
notes: Abstract: 'global flare of mantle-derived magmatism at ~2.75 Ga'; 'proto-cratonic flood basalts'. t_err is a rounding allowance.

title: Oldest known reversal of Earth's magnetic field
text: Flood basalts erupted in Western Australia's Pilbara between 2,775 and 2,715 million years ago froze in a stretch of reversed magnetic polarity, the oldest known flip of north and south. The same rocks show the Pilbara drifting about 27° in latitude, faster than continents move today.
notes: Succession dated c. 2775-2715 Ma; t = midpoint, t_err = half range. Exact age of the reversed interval within it not given in the abstract.

title: Methane-eating microbes in Tumbiana lake stromatolites
text: Stromatolites built on the floors of lakes in Western Australia hold organic matter extremely poor in carbon-13. It points to microbes that lived by eating methane, using sulfur compounds instead of oxygen.
notes: lepot2019 abstract: 2.72 Ga lacustrine stromatolites, Tumbiana Formation; δ13Corg -56 to -51 ‰; S-fueled anaerobic methane oxidation. t_err is a rounding allowance.

title: Molecular fossils of the oldest eukaryotes turn out to be contamination
text: Steroid and hopane molecules in 2.7-billion-year-old Pilbara shales were long the oldest evidence of eukaryotes and oxygen-making cyanobacteria. Isotope work and ultraclean drill cores showed the molecules were younger contamination.

title: Fossil raindrops weigh the ancient air
text: Raindrop imprints in 2.7-billion-year-old volcanic ash in South Africa show air density was less than twice today's, ruling out a very thick atmosphere as the answer to the faint young Sun puzzle.

title: Air pressure less than half today's
text: Fossil gas bubbles in 2.7-billion-year-old lava flows show that atmospheric pressure was less than half of modern levels.

title: Kenoran orogeny folds the Superior craton
text: Folding, peak metamorphism and gold deposits across North America's Superior craton date to 2.72–2.66 billion years ago. In Wyoming's Teton Range, rocks record a Himalaya-style collision of continents between 2.70 and 2.68 billion years ago.
notes: Just after the 326-374 stretch (page 377). snyder2021 abstract: Kenoran (D2) deformation with Au mineralization and peak metamorphism 2.72-2.66 Ga; swapp2018 abstract: 2.70-2.68 Ga Himalayan-style orogeny. t = midpoint of 2.72-2.66.

title: Jeerinah impact: ejecta spread over two continents
text: A large asteroid hit a partly continental target. Its melt droplets, iridium and the oldest known shocked quartz in distant ejecta form a millimetre-thin layer in Pilbara shale, likely the same layer as in Carawine (Australia) and Monteville (South Africa). It is the first of at least three impacts recorded between 2.63 and 2.49 billion years ago. The second left a spherule layer in the Wittenoom Formation, below an ash bed dated 2,504 million years.
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: wittenoom-impact (rasmussen2005).

title: One Kenorland, or several supercratons?
text: About 35 large pieces of Archean crust survive, most with rifted edges: fragments of bigger landmasses. One view joins them all in a single supercontinent, Kenorland. Another sees separate supercratons with their own histories: Superia (Superior), Vaalbara (Kaapvaal) and Sclavia (Slave craton), assembled by about 2.6 billion years ago.

title: An orange organic haze comes and goes
text: Sulfur and carbon isotopes indicate the late Archean sky repeatedly switched into a methane-rich state with an organic haze, like Titan's, and back.

title: The Great Dyke slices across Zimbabwe
text: Magma fills a crack about 550 km long and up to 11 km wide across the Zimbabwe craton, together with two satellite dykes, all within a few million years of 2574 Ma. Its layered rocks hold the world's second-largest platinum resource, after the Bushveld Complex.

title: A vast carbonate platform grows on the Kaapvaal craton
text: The Campbellrand–Malmani platform of South Africa builds up largely from crystals that grew straight on the seafloor: aragonite fans and calcite crusts up to decimetres thick. Seawater must have been supersaturated in calcium carbonate, unlike any younger ocean.

title: Giant sulfur bacteria fossilized in deep-water chert
text: Black chert of the Gamohaan Formation, South Africa, holds unusually large spherical microfossils, 20–265 µm across. Their size, setting and sulfur isotopes suggest sulfur-oxidizing bacteria like the modern _Thiomargarita_: the oldest reported fossil sulfur bacteria.

title: Another whiff of oxygen
text: Molybdenum and rhenium in a 2.5-billion-year-old shale record a brief rise in oxygen shortly before the Great Oxidation Event.

title: Banded iron formations at their peak
text: Huge banded iron formations, the source of much of the world's iron ore, are laid down in iron-rich, oxygen-poor seas around the end of the Archean. In Western Australia the Hamersley Group's run of banded iron begins with the 230 m Marra Mamba Iron Formation, its top dated 2,597 ± 5 million years.
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: marra-mamba-iron-formation (trendall1998).

title: An asteroid over 10 km across leaves ejecta in iron formations
text: Spherule layers in the Dales Gorge (Australia) and Kuruman (South Africa) banded iron formations, laid down at the same time, both carry meteoritic iridium: likely one impact. The rocks above show no lasting change, so even large impacts did not always reset the surface environment.

title: The Moon is 60,000 km closer and a day lasts 16.9 hours
text: Climate cycles preserved in banded iron formation of Western Australia show the Moon about 321,800 km away (today about 384,300 km), a day of 16.9 ± 0.2 hours, and a precession cycle of about 11,000 years instead of today's 21,000.

title: Superia begins to break apart
text: Rifting of the Superior craton's ancestral landmass starts about 2.45 billion years ago; Sclavia holds together until after 2.23 billion. The freed cratons drift alone for some 200 million years before joining Laurentia, the core of North America, 2.0–1.8 billion years ago.

title: Ongeluk eruptions and the first global glaciation
text: Lavas of the Ongeluk large igneous province erupt near the equator in southern Africa about 2,426 million years ago. Their age also dates the oldest Paleoproterozoic global (Makganyene) glaciation and the onset of significant oxygen in the air.

title: Kalahari manganese: the largest deposit on land
text: Around 2.4 billion years ago, iron and manganese layers build up on the seafloor of the Kaapvaal craton in South Africa: the Hotazel Formation, the oldest large chemical manganese deposit and the biggest land-based one on Earth. Metals from hydrothermal plumes were oxidized, mostly with the help of microbes, near the start of the Great Oxidation.

title: Fungus-like threads inside 2.4-billion-year-old lava
text: Gas bubbles in Ongeluk basalt from South Africa hold branching, tangled filaments like the fungal mycelia found in younger volcanic rock under the sea. If they are fungi, the group is two to three times older than thought and began in the deep biosphere, not on land; they may instead be an unknown fungus-like branch.

title: An ozone layer forms and locks in the oxygen
text: Once oxygen passes about 1/100,000 of today's level, ozone begins to shield the lower air from ultraviolet light, so oxygen lasts longer and builds up faster. A model shows this feedback can flip the atmosphere from a low-oxygen state to a high one: a possible switch behind the Great Oxidation.
notes: goldblatt2006 dates the Great Oxidation 'approximately 2.4 billion years ago'; the book's GOE entry is 2.32 Ga (bekker2004).

title: Arrowsmith orogeny: mountain-building in a quiet age
text: On the northwest margin of the Rae craton in northern Canada, a long-lived collision belt (2.5–2.3 billion years old) melts deep crust around 2.38 billion years ago; granites keep forming until 2.31 billion. It is one of the few records of mountain-building during the global magmatic lull.

title: A giant fan of dykes spreads across southern India
text: Within about 5 million years, around 2,367 million years ago, magma fills cracks over 140,000 km² of the Dharwar craton. The dykes fan out through 40° from a focal point some 300 km to the west, likely above the head of a mantle plume.

title: Huronian glaciations: the first great ice ages
text: Repeated glaciations spread ice to low latitudes as oxygen rises and methane falls during the Great Oxidation Event. Volcanic ash in Ontario's Cobalt Group, which holds the third and youngest glacial unit, dates to about 2,310 million years ago.
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: gordon-lake-ash (rasmussen2024).

title: A quiet Earth? The great magmatic lull
text: Zircon ages suggest that volcanism and crust-building slowed sharply from about 2.45 billion years ago for 200–250 million years: few new island arcs, little new crust, a gap in banded iron. One idea is that plate motions largely stalled. Busy belts in Canada and China, such as a volcanic arc at Xiong'ershan 2.33–2.27 billion years ago, question how quiet it really was.
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: xiongershan-arc (liu2024).

title: Oxygen has risen in the atmosphere
text: Sulfur isotopes show the end of the oxygen-free atmosphere by about 2.32 billion years ago: the Great Oxidation Event.

title: Oxygen rises and falls for 100 million more years
text: After 2.32 billion years ago, sulfur and iron records from South Africa show air oxygen still swinging above and below a trace level with each change in ocean chemistry and climate. It stays up for good only around 2.22 billion years ago.
notes: poulton2021: oscillations across 1e-5 PAL for ~200 Myr (from ~2.43 Ga), permanent ~2.22 Ga with Lomagundi. gumsley2017: oscillations until <=2,250-2,240 Ma. Dig 452-468.

title: Malley dykes cut the Slave craton
text: Diabase dykes cut the Slave craton of northern Canada 2,231 million years ago. Their magnetism shows the Slave and Superior cratons were probably not parts of one supercontinent at this time; Sclavia, the Slave's ancestral landmass, breaks up only after 2.23 billion years ago.
notes: buchan2012 abstract: 2231 ± 2 Ma, U-Pb baddeleyite; Slave and Superior not drifting together 2.23-2.03 Ga. bleeker2003 verification: Sclavia did not break up before 2.23 Ga, break-up 2.2-2.0 Ga. Dig 452-468.

title: Yarrabubba: Earth's oldest known impact structure
text: A 70 km impact structure in Western Australia, dated from shock-recrystallized monazite and zircon, is the oldest recognized meteorite impact structure on Earth.

title: Oldest secure fossils of cyanobacteria
text: Once 2.7-billion-year-old molecular fossils were shown to be contamination, the oldest fossil evidence of cyanobacteria, the oxygen makers, reverted to about 2.15 billion years ago.

title: Lomagundi excursion: the largest carbon-isotope shift
text: Carbonate rocks worldwide record a huge positive carbon-isotope excursion, read as massive burial of organic carbon that released 12–22 times today's atmospheric oxygen inventory over 160 million years.

title: Francevillian fossils: colonial life 2.1 billion years ago?
text: Centimetre-sized, lobed fossils in Gabon's Francevillian shales suggest large colonial organisms with coordinated growth. Their biological nature is debated.

title: Bushveld Complex: the world's largest layered intrusion
text: A vast body of magma crystallizes in layers beneath the Kaapvaal craton of South Africa, alongside magmatism across the northern craton and Botswana. Its Merensky Reef and other layers hold most of the world's known platinum-group metals, chromium and vanadium.

title: Late lava on the Moon: the Chang'e-5 basalts
text: Basalt returned by Chang'e-5 erupted 2,030 million years ago, long after most lunar volcanism had ended around 2.9–2.8 billion years ago. The youngest lunar volcanic rock dated from samples.

title: Vredefort impact, South Africa
text: An asteroid strikes what is now South Africa. Zircons shock-metamorphosed and melted by the impact date the Vredefort structure to 2,023 million years ago.

title: Purtuniq ophiolite: a slice of 2-billion-year-old ocean floor
text: Thrust sheets in the Cape Smith belt of northern Quebec preserve pillow lavas, sheeted dykes and gabbros of oceanic crust formed at a spreading ridge about 1,998 million years ago. With a younger, Hawaii-like suite on top, the section is more than 9 km thick: ancient ridge crust was at least as thick as today's.

title: Earliest phosphorite deposits
text: The oldest known phosphorus-rich sediments formed in the Zaonega Formation of Karelia about 2 billion years ago, some 300 million years after oxygen first built up in the air. Phosphatized microfossils resembling sulphur bacteria suggest that microbes helped precipitate the phosphate, as they do at modern seeps and upwelling zones.

title: Karelia's Zaonega sea buries carbon, later cooked into shungite
text: In the Onega Basin of Russian Karelia, muds rich in organic carbon piled up between about 1,975 and 1,968 million years ago, alongside lava flows. Heat later turned the organic matter into petroleum and then into shungite, a black rock of almost pure carbon: the remains of a 2-billion-year-old oil field.

title: Glenburgh Orogeny: the Yilgarn Craton collides with the Pilbara
text: An ocean closed and the Yilgarn Craton collided with the Pilbara Craton and the Glenburgh Terrane between about 1,965 and 1,950 million years ago. The collision completed the West Australian Craton.

title: Supercontinent Columbia (Nuna) assembles
text: Mountain belts formed 2.1–1.8 billion years ago on nearly every continent record the collisions that built Columbia, a supercontinent older than Rodinia.

title: Jormua ophiolite: a Red Sea–style ocean opens in Finland
text: In northeastern Finland, the Jormua ophiolite preserves a fragment of oceanic crust formed about 1,950 million years ago as a continent rifted apart, like the young Red Sea today. Its basalts show no sign of a subduction-related origin.

title: Snowbird eclogites: continental crust pulled down to mantle depths
text: In northern Saskatchewan, eclogites record rock squeezed at pressures of at least 1.8–2.0 GPa and heated to 920–1,000 °C; zircon dates this peak to 1,904.0 ± 0.3 million years ago. They show continental crust subducted deep into the mantle, then rising back quickly because it was buoyant.

title: Sagittarius dwarf galaxy plunges through the Milky Way's disk
text: Stars near the Sun formed in a burst about 1.9 billion years ago, one of three dated bursts (5.7, 1.9 and 1.0 billion years ago) that coincide with passages of the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy. The link is suggestive, not proven.

title: _Grypania_: a coiled ribbon, possibly the oldest alga
text: Coiled, centimetre-scale ribbons in Michigan's Negaunee Iron Formation may be early eukaryotic algae. First dated to about 2.1 billion years, the formation was later tied to a volcanic layer dated at 1,874 ± 9 million years. Debated.
notes: Later redating suggests ~1.87 Ga; find a citable source.

title: Sudbury impact, Ontario
text: Zircon dating places the impact that formed the Sudbury structure in Canada at 1,850 million years ago, one of the few precisely dated Precambrian impacts.

title: The deep ocean turns sulfidic
text: Banded iron formations stop forming about 1.84 billion years ago as the deep ocean becomes rich in hydrogen sulfide rather than iron. Sulfidic conditions may have lasted until a second rise in oxygen 0.8–0.58 billion years ago.

title: Avanavero dolerites flood the Guiana Shield
text: Sills and dykes of dolerite, the Avanavero large igneous province, intrude the Guiana Shield of northern South America, some into the sedimentary rocks of the Roraima Supergroup. Baddeleyite crystals date them to 1,795 ± 2 and 1,793 ± 1 million years. Their magnetism suggests Amazonia lay next to Laurentia and Baltica, perhaps at the core of the supercontinent Columbia.
notes: reis2013 abstract (via ISC index page): U-Pb ID-TIMS baddeleyite 1795 ± 2 and 1793 ± 1 Ma (Pakaraima, Urupi blocks), Guyana dyke 1794 ± 4 Ma; some intrude Roraima Supergroup and Urupi Fm; palaeomagnetism supports Laurentia/Baltica/Amazonia link at 1.79 Ga, possibly core of Columbia. Dig 556-568.

title: The Xiong'er lavas and a giant dyke swarm flood North China
text: Along the southern edge of the North China craton, 3–7 km of lava, from basalt to rhyolite, piles up over more than 60,000 km², while a swarm of dykes cuts across more than 100,000 km² of the craton's interior. Together they form a large igneous province 1.78 billion years old, which its describers attribute to a mantle plume.
notes: peng2008 abstract (via ISC index page): XVP 1.78 Ga, > 0.06 M km2, 3-7 km of extrusives, basalt to rhyolite; NCDS coeval, outcrop > 0.1 M km2; combined LIP > 0.1 M km3; mantle plume favoured. Dig 556-568.

title: Complex cells already bud, form colonies and open their cysts
text: Microfossils in the 1.78–1.73-billion-year-old McDermott Formation of northern Australia have shapes that need a cytoskeleton and internal membranes. Some reproduced by budding, formed simple multicellular clusters or opened their cyst walls, and some may have eaten other cells. Their describer argues the last common ancestor of all eukaryotes is older than 1.75 billion years; molecular clocks place it anywhere from 1.2 to over 1.8 billion.
notes: javaux2025 abstract (Europe PMC): 1.78-1.73 Ga McDermott Fm, McArthur Basin; complexity requires cytoskeleton and endomembrane system; pushes minimum age of uncontested eukaryote fossils back >100 Myr; budding, simple multicellularity, programmed cyst openings, possible eukaryovory and ectosymbiosis; LECA >1.75 Ga. brocks2023 abstract: molecular clocks put LECA between ~1.2 and >1.8 Ga. Dig 556-568.

title: Gold arrives at Homestake, the mine that later caught neutrinos from the Sun
text: Gold is carried into the rocks of the Black Hills at Homestake, one of the largest hydrothermal gold deposits known, from which more than 40 million ounces have been mined. Arsenopyrite from the ore gives a rhenium–osmium age of 1,736 ± 8 million years, as blocks of the crust began to be uplifted. From 1970 the Homestake mine at Lead also housed a chlorine detector counting neutrinos from the Sun.
notes: morelli2010 abstract (JCU ResearchOnline): one of the largest known hydrothermal gold deposits, >40 Moz Au produced; arsenopyrite Re-Os 1736 ± 8 Ma (MSWD 1.6); gold introduced ca. 1730 Ma, coincident with onset of exhumation of crustal blocks. Dig 556-568. Neutrino detector: davis1990 abstract ('in the Homestake mine, Lead, SD', 1970–1988) and cleveland1998 abstract ('since 1970'). added 2026-11-23.

title: Oldest secure fossils of complex cells
text: With the Archean molecular evidence discarded, the oldest fossil evidence for eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus, dates to 1.78–1.68 billion years ago.

title: Grand Canyon basement rocks are baked deep in the crust
text: Volcanic and sedimentary rocks laid down 1,750–1,741 million years ago, now exposed in the Grand Canyon's Upper Granite Gorge, are buried and heated, in places to granulite grade; monazite grown in them dates the peak to 1,706–1,697 Ma. Granite and pegmatite dykes injected between 1,698 and 1,662 Ma locally make up half of the rock.

title: Australia's giant lead–zinc–silver ores form
text: Over some 50 million years, giant lead–zinc–silver ore bodies form in muddy basins of Australia: Broken Hill (New South Wales; ash beside the ore dated 1,685 ± 3 million years), then Mount Isa and Hilton in Queensland (host shales 1,654–1,652 million years old) and McArthur River in the Northern Territory (about 1,640 million). Their metals were laid down with the sediment or soon after burial. Sullivan in British Columbia, unusually rich in tin, followed 1,475 ± 4 million years ago.
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: broken-hill-ore (page2005), mcarthur-river-zinc (page1998), sullivan-ore (slack2020). Span = Broken Hill to McArthur River.

title: An early menagerie of single-celled eukaryotes in North China
text: Black shales of the lower Changcheng Group, 1,673–1,638 million years old, preserve 15 species of organic-walled microfossils. Six, among them _Germinosphaera_, _Dictyosphaera_ and _Valeria_, are unambiguous eukaryotes: cells with a nucleus were already moderately diverse.

title: Mazatzal orogeny: island arcs crushed onto southern Laurentia
text: A string of island arcs and the basins between them are squeezed onto the southern edge of Laurentia, in what is now Arizona and New Mexico, mainly between 1,654 and 1,643 million years ago. The arcs' granites, 1,680–1,650 Ma old, are new crust drawn from the mantle.

title: Molecular fossils of a lost world of early complex life
text: Shales of the Barney Creek Formation, northern Australia, hold 'protosterols': primitive steroid molecules made by extinct stem-group eukaryotes. They suggest early complex cells were common for hundreds of millions of years before modern eukaryote groups took over.

title: Purple and green sulfur bacteria in a stagnant sea
text: Molecular fossils in a 1.64-billion-year-old basin in northern Australia come from purple and green sulfur bacteria, microbes that live where sunlit water has no oxygen and is rich in hydrogen sulfide.

title: _Qingshania_: oldest known multicellular eukaryote
text: Unbranched filaments of cells up to 190 µm wide, some holding possible spores, are preserved in the Chuanlinggou Formation of North China. They imply eukaryotes became multicellular early in their history, though which group they belong to is unclear.

title: The Wiborg batholith: rapakivi, the granite of St Petersburg
text: Huge bodies of granite crystallise beneath southeast Finland and Russian Karelia over some 15 million years. Their pale ovoid feldspar crystals rimmed with plagioclase define 'rapakivi' granite; Wiborg is its type locality. Quarried near Virolahti, it went into St Petersburg's grandest structures from 1760 to 1917, among them the Alexander Column and the 112 columns of St Isaac's Cathedral; it is still sold worldwide as polished stone such as Baltic Brown.
notes: Building-stone facts from bulakh2020 abstract, added 2026-11-23.

title: A bacterium moves in: the origin of mitochondria
text: A free-living alphaproteobacterium is taken up by another cell and becomes the mitochondrion, the power plant of complex cells. Molecular clocks calibrated with fossils put this between 2.05 and 1.21 billion years ago; modern eukaryotes arise after 1.84 billion.

title: Worm burrows 1.6 billion years old? The Chorhat claim
text: Grooves in the Chorhat Sandstone of India were described in 1998 as tunnels of worm-like animals mining under microbial mats. Zircon dating then put the rock at 1.6 billion years, a billion years before any accepted animal, and the burrows remain unconfirmed; their biological origin has been questioned.

title: Possible red algae, 400 million years ahead of schedule
text: X-ray tomography of fossils in phosphorite of the Tirohan Dolomite, central India, shows cell walls and what look like pyrenoids in filaments (_Rafatazmia_) and lobed thalli (_Ramathallus_). If they are red algae, crown-group eukaryotes are far older than thought; without DNA this remains debated.

title: Flood rhyolites bury South Australia
text: The Gawler Range Volcanics, a silicic large igneous province, erupt in under 10 million years; their vast rhyolite sheets may have gone out in 260,000 years or less. The same burst of magmatism is linked to the giant Olympic Dam copper–uranium–gold deposit.

title: A pulse of oxygen in the Mesoproterozoic sea
text: Carbonates of the Gaoyuzhuang Formation, North China, record shelf waters becoming progressively oxygenated from about 1,570 million years ago, just before large multicellular eukaryotes appear in the same basin. How widespread the event was is debated.

title: Ribbons of life 30 cm long on a Chinese seafloor
text: Carbonaceous blades up to 30 cm long and 8 cm wide, built of sheets of 10 µm cells, lie in the Gaoyuzhuang Formation. They were probably photosynthetic multicellular eukaryotes, giant for their time, but their place in the tree of life is uncertain.

title: Complex single-celled eukaryotes diversify
text: Microfossils with ornate walls and spines in the 1.5-billion-year-old Roper Group of Australia show eukaryotic cells already varied in form and ecology.

title: The day stalls at about 19 hours
text: A compilation of day-length measurements suggests Earth's spin stopped slowing for about a billion years: a solar tide in the atmosphere pushed back against the Moon's braking. The stall overlaps the 'boring billion' of slow evolution. Debated.

title: _Horodyskia_: a string of beads, fossil or mud?
text: Strings of millimetre-sized beads, up to 15 cm long, cover bedding planes of the Appekunny Formation in Montana and Alberta. Named _Horodyskia moniliformis_ in 2000 and counted by some among the oldest eukaryotes, they were reinterpreted in 2019 as mud flocs caught on tufts of a microbial mat.

title: Oxygen reaches most of the seafloor?
text: Manganese- and iron-rich rocks of the Tieling Formation, North China, about 1,440–1,450 million years old, record molybdenum isotopes heavier than the usual Mesoproterozoic baseline. Modelling suggests up to 80% of the global seafloor was oxygenated: a broader pulse than the local oxygen oases seen elsewhere in this era, though how global it was is debated.

title: A North American granite turns up in Antarctica
text: A glacial boulder of A-type granite found in Antarctica crystallized about 1,440 million years ago, and its chemistry and hafnium and neodymium isotopes match the distinctive granites of that age in North America. East Antarctica must hold granites like them, a sign that the two continents were neighbours.

title: The Belt basin fills with 15–20 km of sediment
text: A deep basin in western Montana and neighbouring Canada fills with the 15–20 km of mud and sand of the Belt Supergroup. Volcanic ash beds dated at 1,454 (at Logan Pass, Glacier National Park), 1,443 and 1,401 million years, above 1,470-million-year-old sills near its base, show that all but its top 1,700 m piled up in only about 70 million years.

title: Supercontinent Columbia (Nuna) breaks up
text: Rifts open along the margins of Laurentia (Belt-Purcell basin), Baltica and Siberia from about 1.6 billion years ago. The break-up ends about 1.3–1.2 billion years ago, marked in North America by the Mackenzie (1.27 billion) and Sudbury (1.24 billion) dyke swarms.

title: Granites and rhyolites spread across North America
text: Granite and rhyolite magmas intrude and erupt across North America, from the midcontinent to the southwest, starting 1,500–1,400 million years ago and generally later towards the west; a younger pulse follows 1,390–1,340 million years ago. Basalt pooling under the crust melted it from below.

title: Milankovitch cycles 1.4 billion years ago: an 18.7-hour day
text: Orbital climate cycles in the Xiamaling Formation of northern China give a day of 18.68 ± 0.25 hours and an Earth–Moon distance of about 341,000 km, the oldest such record when published.

title: The Moon's magnetic field dies
text: Lunar breccias that cooled in a near-zero field show the Moon's core dynamo stopped sometime between about 1.92 and 0.80 billion years ago, probably after a long late phase powered by the crystallizing core.

title: A billion years of thin oxygen
text: Chromium isotopes in sediments from China, Australia and North America show little oxidation at Earth's surface from 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago: oxygen in the air was at most 0.1% of today's. This may explain why animals appeared so late. Short oxygen pulses are debated.

title: Argyle: the world's biggest diamond source erupts
text: The Argyle lamproite in Western Australia, the world's largest source of natural diamonds, erupted between 1,311 and 1,257 million years ago. Stretching of the crust as the supercontinent Columbia (Nuna) broke up let small batches of melt rise through an old, weak rift zone.

title: Mackenzie hotspot: a giant dyke swarm across Canada
text: A mantle plume feeds the Mackenzie large igneous province in northern Canada, with lava flows, sills and a vast fan of dykes, as an ocean begins to open.

title: Eukaryotes gain chloroplasts? (molecular clock)
text: A molecular clock calibrated on the 1,047-million-year-old red alga _Bangiomorpha_ puts the origin of photosynthesis in eukaryotes, the endosymbiosis that produced the chloroplast, at about 1.25 billion years ago. Older fossils interpreted as red algae, about 1.6 billion years old, would push it earlier.

title: Earth's solid inner core begins to grow? (early estimate)
text: A rise in field strength recorded in rocks has been read as the start of inner-core freezing in the Mesoproterozoic, 1.5–1 billion years ago. Others place it in the Ediacaran; debated.

title: An asteroid hits Scotland: the Stac Fada impact
text: A layer of melt and debris thrown out by an impact lies among the Stoer Group sandstones of northwest Scotland. It is dated to 1,177 ± 5 million years from feldspar that grew from hot fluids in the fresh ejecta, beside an evaporating lake. The crater has not been found; a buried structure under a gravity low about 50 km to the east has been proposed.

title: Musgrave Orogeny: a hundred million years of red-hot crust
text: In central Australia the crust stays at ultrahigh temperatures from about 1,220 to 1,120 million years ago. Granites intrude at 1,000 °C or more across over 15,000 km², fed largely by melts from the mantle while the region is stretched and thinned.

title: The Grenville mountains build up in three stages
text: From the Adirondacks to the southern Appalachians and Texas, the margin of ancestral North America records the same three mountain-building episodes: the Elzevirian (about 1,250–1,220 million years ago), the Shawinigan (1,200–1,140) and the Grenvillian (1,090–980). Together they built the Grenville orogen.

title: Premier kimberlite: the pipe of the Cullinan diamond erupts
text: About 1,150 million years ago a kimberlite pipe erupts through the Kaapvaal craton of South Africa, carrying up rock from the base of the continent at 200 km depth. Its mine produced the Cullinan, the largest gem diamond ever found; such giant diamonds grew from metallic iron–carbon liquid deep in the mantle.
notes: Not in either abstract: that the Cullinan diamond came from the Premier mine, and that it is the largest gem diamond found. Kimberlite age 'c. 1150 Ma' (tappe2021); t_err is a placeholder.

title: Umkondo: one flood of magma across two continents
text: From 1,112 to 1,106 million years ago, magma spreads through two million square kilometres of the Kalahari craton in southern Africa, during the same magnetic polarity interval as the great eruptions in North America. The two are probably parts of one large igneous province, erupted while Rodinia was being assembled.

title: Fossil chlorophyll: an ocean run by tiny cyanobacteria
text: Molecular remains of chlorophyll in 1.1-billion-year-old marine rocks show, from their nitrogen isotopes, that cyanobacteria dominated the ocean's primary producers and larger algae were scarce. Small cells at the base of the food chain may have held back the rise of large, complex life.

title: Supercontinent Rodinia assembles
text: Collisions between about 1.3 and 0.9 billion years ago gather most continents into Rodinia, with Laurentia (ancestral North America) at its core.

title: Midcontinent Rift: North America nearly splits in two
text: From 1,109 to 1,083 million years ago lava pours out along a rift through the middle of North America, around today's Lake Superior, but the continent never breaks apart. Magnetism frozen in the lavas shows the continent racing from high to low latitudes at more than 27 cm a year, before the Grenvillian collisions (1,090–980 million years ago) helped assemble Rodinia. Just before, about 1,098 million years ago, a brief plume pulse injected thick sills beneath the Grand Canyon and Death Valley.
notes: Merged 2026-11-23: midcontinent-rift-plume (mohr2024).

title: A Precambrian superchron: the field stops flipping, then flips wildly
text: Rocks of the Talakh-Khaya section in eastern Siberia, near the end of the Mesoproterozoic, record 33 reversals followed by one long normal-polarity interval: a proposed superchron. Slightly younger Ural rocks record over 40 polarity intervals, perhaps 5–10 reversals per million years. Sharp switches between calm and frantic reversing may be typical of the Precambrian field.
notes: Abstract dates the sections only as ~1100-800 Ma; date of the Talakh-Khaya interval needs the full text.

title: _Bangiomorpha_: red algae and the first known sex
text: Re-dated to 1.047 billion years, this multicellular red alga is the oldest securely identified photosynthetic eukaryote and among the earliest organisms with sexual reproduction.

title: _Proterocladus_: a billion-year-old green seaweed
text: Branching, multicellular green algae from northern China show chlorophytes, cousins of the lineage that later gave rise to land plants, were already large and multicellular.

title: Sagittarius dwarf galaxy passes again; a burst of nearby star formation
text: A third dated burst of star formation in the Sun's neighbourhood coincides with another passage of the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy through the Milky Way's disk.

title: Giant impact on asteroid Vesta carves the Rheasilvia basin
text: An impact gouges a basin about 500 km across at Vesta's south pole, nearly the width of the asteroid. Dawn crater counts date it to about 1 billion years ago, though the age depends on the cratering model used.

title: _Ourasphaira_: the oldest fungi
text: Multicellular microfossils from Arctic Canada, about 1,010–890 million years old, are identified as fungi, more than half a billion years older than earlier undoubted fungal fossils.

title: Tides in Utah record a day of about 18.9 hours
text: Tidal laminae in Utah's Big Cottonwood Formation, roughly 1.0 billion to 800 million years old, record daily, monthly and yearly tide cycles. Counted layers give a day of about 18.9 hours and a Moon already retreating at close to today's rate.

title: Sponges in 890-million-year-old reefs? Perhaps the oldest animals
text: Reefs built by cyanobacteria in northwestern Canada contain a worm-like mesh of tubes identical to the fossil tissue of horny (keratose) sponges. If it is sponge, it is the oldest animal body fossil known, older than the Snowball Earth glaciations; the identification is debated.

title: Manso dykes pin down West Africa's place in Rodinia
text: Dolerite dykes in Ghana, about 860 million years old, preserve the direction of Earth's magnetic field. This first reliable Tonian pole puts West Africa at high latitude, probably joined to Baltica, Amazonia and Congo–São Francisco from about 1.2 to 0.8 billion years ago.

title: A mantle plume? Gairdner dykes and their South China twins
text: The Gairdner dyke swarm of South Australia intrudes 827 ± 6 million years ago, and dykes and sills in South China are the same age (828 ± 7). Both are read as products of a mantle plume that may have started the rifting of Rodinia; the plume interpretation is debated.

title: Copernicus crater forms on the Moon
text: The bright-rayed crater Copernicus is dated to 800 million years ago from ray material sampled by Apollo.

title: Rodinia breaks apart
text: Rifting tears Rodinia apart between about 825 and 740 million years ago, opening new oceans shortly before the Snowball Earth glaciations.

title: The phosphorus cycle shifts
text: Phosphorus in marine rocks stays low for most of Earth's history, then jumps in the late Proterozoic, alongside changes in ocean oxygen, the Snowball glaciations and the emergence of animals.

title: Franklin lavas erupt as the Sturtian Snowball begins
text: The Franklin large igneous province of Arctic Canada erupts at almost exactly the start of the Sturtian glaciation, about 717 million years ago.

title: Sturtian glaciation: Snowball Earth
text: Ice reaches the tropics and persists for 57–59 million years, nearly as long as the whole Cenozoic. The Snowball Earth hypothesis holds that the oceans froze over nearly completely.

title: Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event
text: A second large rise in oxygen during the late Neoproterozoic brings the deep ocean and the air closer to modern levels, around the time animals appear.

title: Algae take over the oceans
text: Steroid biomarkers show algae rising to ecological dominance between the two Snowball glaciations, providing food webs that may have helped animals emerge.

title: Sponge molecules: the first trace of animals?
text: Distinctive steroids in Cryogenian rocks of Oman, laid down no later than the warm interval between the two Snowball glaciations, are attributed to demosponges, which would make them the oldest evidence of animals. Debated.

title: Where are Earth's old craters?
text: Earth has almost no impact craters older than 650 million years, which may mean a massive global erosion event near that time. Debated.

title: Gondwana assembles
text: The southern supercontinent comes together in stages. Eastern Africa collides with pieces of Madagascar, India, Sri Lanka and East Antarctica in the East African Orogen (about 750–620 million years ago); Australia joins in the Kuunga Orogeny (570–530 million). East Gondwana exists only from the Cambrian.

title: Marinoan glaciation: the second Snowball
text: A second global glaciation ends abruptly 635 million years ago, capped worldwide by carbonate rocks laid down in a hot aftermath.

title: Gaskiers glaciation, then the first large Ediacaran fossils
text: A short glaciation lasting less than about 340,000 years is followed within 9.5 million years by the first appearance of large Ediacaran organisms.

title: First large Ediacaran organisms
text: Large, frond-like Ediacaran organisms appear in Newfoundland within 9.5 million years after the Gaskiers glaciation, among the first big multicellular life.
notes: 571 Ma from memory; check Pu 2016.

title: Shuram excursion: the carbon cycle's biggest upheaval?
text: Carbon isotopes swing to their most negative values in the rock record, possibly the largest disturbance of the global carbon cycle. Dating shows the excursion was global and synchronous, and not tied to the rise of the earliest animal ecosystems.

title: Earth's magnetic field nearly collapses
text: Crystals in 565-million-year-old Quebec anorthosites record a field ten times weaker than today's, suggesting the solid inner core had not yet formed and began growing soon after. Debated.

title: _Haootia_: the oldest muscles, in an early cnidarian
text: An impression from Newfoundland shows twisted bundles of fibres arranged in four, with forking corner branches, like the muscles of living stalked jellyfish (Staurozoa). It may be the earliest body fossil of muscle tissue and of a true animal with tissues (eumetazoan).

title: Pannotia: a short-lived supercontinent, or none?
text: Mountain building, new passive margins and climate and sea-level signals around the Precambrian–Cambrian transition have been read as the brief assembly and break-up of a supercontinent, Pannotia. Critics find the evidence tied up with the assembly of Gondwana and doubt Pannotia existed.

title: _Dickinsonia_ was an animal
text: Cholesterol-derived steroids preserved with _Dickinsonia_ fossils show this flat Ediacaran organism was one of the earliest known animals.

art.caption: _Dickinsonia_, an oval, segmented Ediacaran organism. Steroid molecules preserved with its fossils identify it as an animal.

title: The first mass extinction of animals
text: About 80% of the Ediacaran organisms of the White Sea assemblage are missing from the following Nama assemblage, a loss comparable to the great extinctions of later times. The same environments are well sampled in both, so the drop is real; survivors with large surface area for their volume hint at falling oxygen.

title: _Cloudina_: the first skeletons build the first animal reefs
text: _Cloudina_, the earliest known animal with a mineral skeleton, lives in seas worldwide. In Namibia's Nama Group its individuals attach and cement to one another into open reef frameworks, facing nutrient-rich currents: possibly a defence against competitors and the first predators.

title: Animals start to dig: the first three-dimensional burrows
text: _Treptichnus_ burrows in the Shibantan beds of China, alongside Ediacara-type fossils, are the earliest known burrow systems that go down into the sediment, not just along it. Digging churns the microbial mats that Ediacaran organisms depended on, and their decline follows.

title: Foraminifera: shelled protists appear
text: Fossil foraminifera appear in the early Cambrian, about when animals first build skeletons. Molecular data suggest a large radiation of unfossilized, single-chambered forms had already happened in the Neoproterozoic.

art.caption: _Globigerina bulloides_, a living planktonic foraminifer. Many-chambered shells like this diversified only from the Carboniferous on.

title: The Cambrian explosion
text: Most animal body plans appear in the fossil record within a few tens of millions of years, although molecular clocks suggest their lineages diverged earlier.

art.caption: _Anomalocaris canadensis_, a radiodont from the Burgess Shale with a pair of spiny grasping appendages at its head.

title: Archaeocyath sponges build the first Cambrian reefs
text: Sponges with chalky skeletons, the archaeocyaths, help build reefs on shallow carbonate platforms, notably in Siberia. Most species were generalists, living on hard or soft bottoms, in the open or in reef crevices: reef-building seems to follow naturally once animals can attach permanently.
notes: zhuravlev2026 analyses Cloudina and archaeocyath occurrences ca 547–521 Ma (earliest Cambrian archaeocyaths); t approximates their early reef span.

title: First vertebrates: Chengjiang fishes
text: _Haikouichthys_ and _Myllokunmingia_, small fish-like animals from the early Cambrian Chengjiang beds of China, are the oldest known vertebrates. Zircons show the beds are no older than about 518 million years.

art.caption: _Haikouichthys ercaicunensis_, a jawless early Cambrian vertebrate from Chengjiang, China.

title: _Anomalocaris_ sees: giant compound eyes
text: Eyes up to 3 cm long, each with more than 16,000 lenses, belong to _Anomalocaris_, the metre-long top predator of Cambrian seas, from the Emu Bay Shale of South Australia. Among the sharpest eyes ever, they show that compound eyes evolved before hard exoskeletons and that visual hunting drove the early predator–prey arms race.

title: Kalkarindji eruptions and an early Cambrian extinction
text: Flood basalts covering much of northern Australia erupt about 511 million years ago, synchronous with the first major extinction of the Cambrian.

title: _Hallucigenia_: a spiny worm that finally got a head
text: New study of the 508-million-year-old Burgess Shale animal found a long head with simple eyes, a ring of mouth plates and a throat lined with teeth, placing it among the relatives of velvet worms.

art.caption: _Hallucigenia sparsa_ walked on soft legs with paired spines on its back.

title: _Opabinia_: five eyes and a nozzle
text: _Opabinia_ of the Burgess Shale, once a famous 'weird wonder' with five eyes and a long, clawed proboscis, is now known as an early relative of arthropods, near _Anomalocaris_ in the family tree. A second opabiniid from Utah shows the group lived through several Cambrian stages.
notes: Date: Burgess Shale taken as Wuliuan (ICS ~506.5–504.5 Ma); not in pates2022's abstract. 'Five eyes, clawed proboscis' is general knowledge (Whittington 1975).

title: First land plants
text: Fragments of spore-bearing tissue from the Middle Ordovician are the earliest direct fossils of plants on land.

title: Moyero Superchron: Ordovician field locked in reverse
text: For some 15–20 million years in the Early and Middle Ordovician the magnetic field stays almost entirely in reversed polarity, the oldest of three known Phanerozoic superchrons.
notes: Span mapped by hand from stage names (Floian to most of Darriwilian) to approximate GTS ages; check.

title: An asteroid shatters; meteorites rain on Ordovician Earth
text: The breakup of the L-chondrite parent body is the largest known asteroid disruption of the last 3 billion years. Its fragments fell on Earth for millions of years and are found as fossil meteorites in Ordovician limestone.

title: The Appalachians begin: the Taconic orogeny
text: Volcanic island arcs crash into the eastern margin of Laurentia (North America) in the Ordovician, the first of three mountain-building episodes that make the Appalachians. The Acadian collisions follow in the Silurian–Devonian, and the Alleghanian, when Gondwana arrives to complete Pangaea, from the late Mississippian into the Permian.
notes: t and t_err span the Ordovician (ogg2020); hatcher2010 dates the Taconic only as Ordovician.

title: The Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event begins
text: Over the whole Ordovician, marine life multiplies in waves: plankton first, then animals of the open sea floor, then reef communities, each at different times in different regions, with whole faunas migrating between them. Not one event but many in sequence.
notes: Span = the Ordovician (ogg2020); servais2018: the GOBE spans the entire Ordovician.

title: Teeth began as touch: the oldest dentine
text: The armour of the early vertebrate _Eriptychius_ carries small tooth-like bumps (odontodes) with large dentine tubules, the oldest known vertebrate dental tissue. Their resemblance to the sense organs of arthropods suggests dentine first evolved to feel. The Cambrian _Anatolepis_, long claimed as older, turns out to be an arthropod.
notes: Middle Ordovician per haridy2025; t and t_err span the Middle Ordovician (ogg2020).

title: The top of Mount Everest is laid down on the sea floor
text: Limestone now at the summit of Everest accumulates in a warm sea on the north Indian margin of Gondwana. Conodonts (tiny tooth-like fossils) in matching strata of southern Tibet date it to the middle Ordovician (Darriwilian). The India–Asia collision later lifts it to the roof of the world.
notes: t = middle–late Darriwilian (ICS 469.4–458.2 Ma).

title: Parental care: ostracods brood their eggs
text: Pyritized ostracods from the Late Ordovician of New York preserve eggs and young inside the shell, the oldest evidence of brood care, a strategy kept for at least 450 million years.

title: Paleozoic seas reach their highest
text: After rising through the Cambrian, sea level peaks in the Late Ordovician, then falls sharply as the Hirnantian ice sheets grow. Paleozoic sea level changes by up to about 125 m.

title: End-Ordovician glaciation and mass extinction
text: A brief, intense glaciation centred on Gondwana chills the tropical seas and drives the first of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions.

title: A gamma-ray burst behind the end-Ordovician extinction?
text: A nearby gamma-ray burst could strip away much of the ozone layer and trigger cooling; one has been proposed as a partial cause of the end-Ordovician extinction. Such bursts are estimated to strike dangerously close two or more times per billion years. Debated.

title: Oldest horseshoe crab
text: _Lunataspis aurora_ from Late Ordovician deposits of Manitoba is the oldest known horseshoe crab, a lineage still alive today.

art.caption: The living horseshoe crab _Limulus polyphemus_. Its lineage goes back at least to the Late Ordovician.

title: Jaws and teeth: the oldest complete jawed fishes
text: Complete fossils from the early Silurian of China, about 436 million years old, are the earliest jawed vertebrates known from whole bodies.

title: Myriapods: among the first animals on land
text: Zircon dating places kampecarid myriapods from Kerrera, Scotland, at about 425 million years, among the oldest known land animals. The oldest millipede with breathing holes, from Cowie, is about 414 million years old.

title: _Cooksonia_: the archetypal early vascular plant
text: Small, smooth stems that fork in two, each tipped with a spore capsule; no leaves. _Cooksonia_ has stomata and water-conducting tubes, so it is a true vascular plant; the smallest specimens were probably too thin to feed themselves and may have depended on a separate gametophyte generation, as mosses do.

art.caption: _Cooksonia_: smooth stems that fork in two, each ending in a single spore capsule.

notes: edwards1992: late Silurian–early Devonian; t and t_err span Ludlow to Lochkovian (ogg2020).

title: _Entelognathus_: an armoured fish with a modern jaw
text: A Silurian placoderm with jaw bones like those of bony fishes links the armoured placoderms to the lineage that includes us.

art.caption: _Entelognathus primordialis_, a Silurian armoured placoderm whose jaw bones resemble those of bony fishes.

title: _Doliodus_: the oldest articulated shark
text: A shark from New Brunswick, Canada, preserved whole with its teeth in place and one of the oldest shark braincases. It also bears paired spines on its pectoral fins, unknown in cartilaginous fishes before. Shark-like scales go back to perhaps 455 million years ago, but bodies are rare.

title: Coelacanths appear
text: _Euporosteus yunnanensis_, the earliest known coelacanth skull, from the Early Devonian of China, already has the modern coelacanth head anatomy, extending it back by about 17 million years.

art.caption: The living coelacanth _Latimeria chalumnae_. Coelacanth skulls of modern form go back to the Early Devonian.

title: The first wood grows in small plants
text: Two small Early Devonian plants grow secondary xylem, wood, the earliest known. They are far too small to need it for support: wood first evolved to move water, and only later held up trees.

title: _Rhyniognatha_: the oldest insect
text: Jaws from the Rhynie chert of Scotland, about 400 million years old, belong to the oldest known insect and suggest flight may have evolved early.

title: Venus is resurfaced by volcanism
text: Almost all of Venus's surface is renewed by lava, after which volcanism and tectonics decline sharply. Crater counts date this to 300–500 million years ago; whether it was a single catastrophe or a gradual process is debated.

title: First footprints: tetrapod tracks in Poland
text: Trackways at Zachełmie record four-limbed animals walking about 392 million years ago, in the early Eifelian, earlier than the oldest tetrapod skeletons.

title: The first forests
text: Fossil root systems at Cairo, New York, include _Archaeopteris_ trees with modern-looking roots, in the oldest known forest.

title: _Runcaria_: a step toward the seed
text: A Middle Devonian plant from Belgium with a seed-like structure, about 20 million years older than the first true seeds.

title: _Wattieza_: the first trees
text: Fossils from Schoharie County, New York, show the famous Gilboa stumps belonged to tree-fern-like trees at least 8 m tall, among the oldest known trees.

title: _Tiktaalik_: a fish with a neck and wrists
text: A Late Devonian fish from Arctic Canada with a flat head, mobile neck and limb-like fins, intermediate between fish and four-legged animals.

art.caption: _Tiktaalik roseae_, a Late Devonian lobe-finned fish from Arctic Canada with sturdy, limb-like front fins and a neck.

title: Late Devonian mass extinction
text: One of the 'Big Five' extinctions strikes reef ecosystems at the Frasnian–Famennian boundary, now dated precisely to about 372 million years ago.

title: _Acanthostega_ and _Ichthyostega_: limbs with seven and eight digits
text: The earliest known tetrapod limbs, from East Greenland, have more than five digits: eight on the forelimb of _Acanthostega_, seven on the hindlimb of _Ichthyostega_. Their shape suggests digits first evolved for life in water, not for walking on land, and five fingers is not the original pattern.
notes: Upper Devonian per coates1990; t and t_err span the Late Devonian (ogg2020). Drawing art/line/acanthostega.svg (PhyloPic, Hartman, CC0) fetched but detached: wide-art layout bug (collision-pages.md).

title: Oldest ocean floor still in place forms
