text: Magnetic stripes beneath the eastern Mediterranean suggest its floor is Paleozoic ocean crust about 340 million years old, the oldest known ocean floor not yet recycled into the mantle.

title: _Arthropleura_: the largest arthropod ever
text: A giant millipede relative more than 2 m long; a 76 cm section of moulted skin from northern England is the largest arthropleurid fossil and the earliest proof of its gigantism.

art.caption: _Arthropleura armata_, the largest arthropod known.

title: Pangaea comes together
text: The collision of Gondwana with Laurussia completes the supercontinent Pangaea in the late Carboniferous, raising the Appalachian–Variscan mountains.

title: Amniotes appear: eggs that can be laid on land
text: The first amniotes, the group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals, appear in the coal-swamp forests. Their shelled, self-contained egg frees them from a water-bound larval stage. Their family soon splits into reptiles and synapsids, the line leading to mammals.

title: _Swillingtonia_: the oldest conifer, preserved as charcoal
text: Tiny leafy shoots from Upper Carboniferous shale in Yorkshire were charred by a wildfire before burial, which kept their cells uncrushed. Their sunken stomata and leaf form match the early conifer _Lebachia_: the earliest record of a conifer.
notes: scott1983 dates it as Westphalian B (regional stage); t ≈ 313 Ma (Duckmantian) is a conversion not checked against a timescale source.

title: Late Paleozoic Ice Age
text: Ice sheets come and go across southern Gondwana for tens of millions of years, the longest ice age of the Phanerozoic.

title: The Tully monster
text: A soft-bodied animal with a long, pincer-tipped snout and eyes on a crossbar, from Mazon Creek, Illinois, about 309–307 million years ago. It has been called a vertebrate and a non-vertebrate; debated.

art.caption: _Tullimonstrum gregarium_, Illinois's state fossil.

title: Carboniferous rainforest collapse
text: The coal-swamp rainforests of Euramerica break up into islands as the climate dries, reshaping the evolution of land vertebrates.

title: Oxygen peaks at its highest level
text: The GEOCARBSULF carbon–sulfur model puts atmospheric oxygen at its all-time high around the Carboniferous–Permian, well above today's 21%. Later models and rock proxies disagree on how high it rose. Debated.

title: Giant insects
text: Griffinflies with wingspans up to about 70 cm fly over Carboniferous and Permian swamps; maximum insect size tracks atmospheric oxygen.

art.caption: _Meganeura_, a giant griffinfly of the late Carboniferous and a distant relative of dragonflies.

title: Did wood-rotting fungi end the coal age?
text: Genome studies trace the enzymes that break down lignin, wood's toughest polymer, to Paleozoic fungi, and some linked their spread to the end of peak coal formation. A study of coal floras found lignin decay was already common, and points to climate and tectonics during Pangaea's assembly instead. Debated.

title: Asteroid impacts on Earth and Moon become more frequent
text: Ages of young lunar craters, estimated from how much of their rocky ejecta survives, suggest the impact rate on the Moon and Earth rose by a factor of about 2.6 near the end of the Paleozoic. Debated.

title: Kiaman Superchron: some 55 million years without a reversal
text: From the late Carboniferous to the late Permian Earth's magnetic field stays in reversed polarity, with no known reversals. Its exact start and end ages are still argued over.
notes: Span 318-265 Ma from memory; check boundaries against Ogg 2020.

title: _Helicoprion_: a jaw with a spiral saw of teeth
text: CT scans show this Late Paleozoic fish's spiral whorl of teeth filled its lower jaw, adding teeth without shedding old ones. It was a ratfish relative, not a shark.

art.caption: _Helicoprion_, a holocephalan with a tooth whorl in its lower jaw.

title: Siberian Traps: lava floods Siberia before the end-Permian extinction
text: One of the largest volcanic outpourings since animals appeared. About two-thirds of the lava and ash erupts within some 300,000 years, before and during the extinction; then magma spreads as sills through the shallow crust, and eruptions go on for at least 500,000 years more, perhaps holding back recovery.
notes: t = end-Permian extinction onset (251.941 Ma, burgess2014) minus the ~300 kyr main eruptive window of burgess2015's abstract.

title: End-Permian mass extinction begins
text: The most severe extinction in Earth history, coinciding with Siberian Traps volcanism; most marine species vanish within roughly sixty thousand years.

title: Land plants come through the Great Dying
text: Early Triassic plant fossils are scarce, which long suggested that plants died out along with animals. Global records of plant fossils and pollen show this is mostly a sampling gap: pollen shows gymnosperms persisting, and plant losses were smaller and more selective than a mass extinction.

title: _Triadobatrachus_: the oldest frog relative
text: A single fossil from the Early Triassic of Madagascar is the earliest known lissamphibian, the group of living amphibians. It mixes frog features with older ones: a longer trunk, a tail and hind legs not built for jumping.
notes: Early Triassic per ascarrunz2016; t and t_err span the Early Triassic (ogg2020). 'Longer trunk' = 15 presacral vertebrae vs frogs' fewer; 'tail' = caudal vertebrae reported.

title: Reef corals team up with algae
text: Small coral-rich patch reefs grow in clear, nutrient-poor shallows of the western Tethys. Growth bands and isotopes in exceptionally preserved corals from the Italian Dolomites show they already hosted algae in their tissues, as modern reef corals do: a partnership in place before the reef boom at the end of the Triassic.
notes: Carnian per frankowiak2021; t and t_err span the Carnian (~237–227 Ma, ogg2020).

title: Dawn of the dinosaurs
text: _Eodromaeus_ and _Eoraptor_ from Argentina's Ischigualasto Formation, about 231 million years old, are among the earliest dinosaurs.

art.caption: _Eoraptor lunensis_, a small, early two-legged dinosaur from the Late Triassic of Argentina.

title: The crocodile line begins: crocodylomorphs appear
text: The group of today's 26 or so crocodiles, alligators, caimans and gharials starts some 230 million years ago. Its Mesozoic members were far more varied: sea-going thalattosuchians, land-dwelling notosuchians, plant-eaters and top predators. Skull variety peaks in the Cretaceous; only the semi-aquatic predators survive.

title: The oldest animals in amber
text: Droplets of 230-million-year-old amber from the Italian Dolomites trap a fly and two gall mites, about 100 million years older than any arthropod previously found in amber.

title: _Odontochelys_: a turtle with half a shell
text: A Late Triassic turtle from China had a full belly shell but no top shell, and still had teeth.

art.caption: _Odontochelys semitestacea_, a toothed Late Triassic turtle with only its lower shell.

title: Pterosaurs: the first vertebrates to fly under power
text: The oldest unambiguous pterosaurs appear in the Late Triassic. Their closest relatives turn out to be lagerpetids, small running dinosaur precursors with no hint of flight, which places pterosaurs firmly on the bird side of the reptile family tree.
notes: Late Triassic per ezcurra2020; t and t_err span 237–201.4 Ma (ogg2020).

title: Manicouagan impact, Quebec
text: Zircons in impact melt date the Manicouagan crater to 214 million years ago, about 12 million years before the end-Triassic extinction, so it probably did not cause it.

title: Pangaea splits; Central Atlantic lavas trigger the end-Triassic extinction
text: Basalts of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province pour out as Pangaea rifts apart. Zircon dates tie the eruptions to the end-Triassic mass extinction, which cleared the way for the dinosaurs.

title: _Mussaurus_: the earliest dinosaur herd and nesting colony
text: In Patagonia, over 100 eggs and 80 skeletons of the early long-necked dinosaur _Mussaurus_, from embryos to adults, lie together. Eggs and hatchlings cluster in a nesting area, and individuals of similar age are grouped: a herd sorted by age. It is the oldest evidence of complex social behaviour in dinosaurs, by at least 40 million years.

title: Dinosaur embryos and parental care
text: Embryos of _Massospondylus_ from the Early Jurassic of South Africa had big heads and forelimbs and no well-developed teeth, suggesting hatchlings walked on four legs and needed parental care.

art.caption: Adult _Massospondylus carinatus_; adults could walk on two legs, unlike their four-legged hatchlings.

title: _Castorocauda_: the oldest fur, on a Jurassic 'beaver'
text: A docodont from the Middle Jurassic of China is the most primitive relative of mammals known to have had fur. It swam and burrowed like a platypus, with a broad, flat, partly scaly tail like a beaver's: early mammal relatives were not all small shrew-like insect-eaters.
notes: ji2006's abstract says Middle Jurassic only; t and t_err span the Middle Jurassic (ogg2020).

title: The oldest known song: a Jurassic katydid
text: Wings of the 165-million-year-old katydid _Archaboilus musicus_ were built to sing a pure musical note at 6.4 kHz, a low call suited to a forest of conifers and giant ferns.

art.caption: _Tettigonia viridissima_, a modern katydid, shown as a relative of the Jurassic singer _Archaboilus musicus_.

title: _Juramaia_: an early relative of placental mammals
text: A shrew-sized Jurassic mammal from China is the oldest known eutherian, the group that includes placental mammals.

art.caption: _Juramaia sinensis_, a shrew-sized Jurassic mammal from China and the oldest known eutherian.

title: Placental and marsupial lines have split
text: _Juramaia_ shows the lineage leading to placental mammals had separated from that of marsupials by about 160 million years ago.

title: Horsetails of a Jurassic hot spring look just like today's
text: _Equisetum thermale_, preserved in place in the San Agustín hot-spring deposit of Patagonia, has every feature of living horsetails. It grew in dense stands in hot, mineral-rich wetlands, showing that modern-type _Equisetum_ existed in the Jurassic, much earlier than molecular clocks suggest.
notes: Upper Jurassic per channing2011; t and t_err span the Late Jurassic (ogg2020).

title: _Archaeopteryx_: feathered dinosaur, early bird
text: Late Jurassic fossils from Germany with toothed jaws, clawed wings and vaned feathers sit near the origin of birds.

art.caption: _Archaeopteryx lithographica_, a Late Jurassic feathered dinosaur from Germany, close to the ancestry of birds.

title: Tamu Massif: Earth's largest single volcano
text: A shield volcano about 650 km across erupts on the Pacific sea floor, forming the oldest and largest part of the Shatsky Rise oceanic plateau. It is the largest single volcano known on Earth.

title: _Archaefructus_: early flowers from China
text: Early Cretaceous plants from Liaoning with seeds enclosed in carpels belong to one of the oldest known flowering-plant families.

art.caption: _Archaefructus liaoningensis_, an Early Cretaceous plant from Liaoning with its seeds enclosed in carpels.

title: _Montsechia_: an early flowering plant
text: An aquatic flowering plant from Spain, Barremian in age (about 124 million years old), is among the oldest known angiosperms.

title: _Ginkgo_: a living fossil
text: A _Ginkgo_ fossil from the Early Cretaceous Yixian Formation of China, more than 121 million years old, looks almost like the living tree: the genus has barely changed for over 100 million years.

art.caption: Leaf of the living _Ginkgo biloba_, sole survivor of its lineage.

title: Diatoms: glass-walled algae flourish
text: The first physical remains of diatoms are Jurassic; well-preserved, diverse diatom floras are known from the Early Cretaceous.

art.caption: _Triceratium_, a centric diatom; early fossil diatoms are all of this radial, centric kind.

title: Ontong Java Nui erupts; the oceans lose their oxygen
text: Undersea eruptions build Ontong Java Nui, a vast volcanic plateau in the western Pacific, over some 5 million years. Their peak coincides with Oceanic Anoxic Event 1a, when black organic-rich mud spreads over stagnant sea floors; osmium isotopes in Italian black shales record the volcanic pulses.

title: A dinosaur's last meal
text: The armoured dinosaur _Borealopelta_ from Alberta, preserved with its stomach contents, had last eaten mostly fern leaves, with some cycads, stems and charcoal: the best evidence of any plant-eating dinosaur's diet.

art.caption: _Borealopelta markmitchelli_, a nodosaur preserved in three dimensions.

title: The South Atlantic splits a salt basin between Brazil and Angola
text: Salt basins now on the shelves of Brazil and of Angola, Congo and Gabon were once one rift basin in the subtropics. It was cut in two about 112 million years ago, at the Aptian–Albian boundary, as seafloor spreading began north of the Walvis Ridge and Rio Grande Rise.

title: Tycho crater forms on the Moon
text: Tycho, the young crater whose bright rays stretch across the full Moon, is dated to 109 million years ago from material sampled by Apollo.

title: Insect pollination before flowers
text: Thrips preserved in Spanish amber carry pollen of gymnosperms, showing insects pollinated plants in the Early Cretaceous.

art.caption: A thrips (order Thysanoptera), shown as a modern example. Thrips in Spanish amber carried gymnosperm pollen in the Early Cretaceous.

title: Cretaceous Normal Superchron: the field stops reversing
text: For about 37 million years the magnetic field keeps normal polarity with almost no reversals, a long quiet stretch in the seafloor's magnetic stripes.

title: Most modern ferns arise in the shadow of flowering plants
text: Ferns were thought to have retreated before the rise of flowering plants. Molecular dating shows the opposite: polypod ferns, more than 80% of fern species alive today, diversify in the Cretaceous after flowering plants, perhaps opportunists in a world that flowering plants were coming to dominate.
notes: schneider2004's abstract says Cretaceous, after angiosperms; t and t_err span 134–66 Ma (post-Archaefructus to end-Cretaceous).

title: Social ants in amber: castes, group hunting and war
text: Burmese amber preserves early ants with separate queen and worker castes, groups of workers recruited together, and two species locked in combat: these ants were already eusocial. Their stem-group lineages later died out, perhaps outcompeted by the ancestors of today's ants with their massive colonies.

title: The Western Interior Seaway joins Arctic and tropical waters
text: A shallow sea floods the middle of North America. Warm Tethyan water has pushed north up the seaway since about 98 million years ago; at peak flooding, 95–94 million years ago, it links up with cold boreal water from the north, mixing and oxygenating the water throughout the seaway and as far south as Suriname.

title: Highest sea level of the Cretaceous
text: In the earliest Turonian, sea level stands roughly 240–250 m above today's, flooding the interiors of continents with shallow seas. Throughout the Cretaceous it stays 75–250 m higher than now.

title: Oceanic Anoxic Event 2: seas lose their oxygen
text: A massive pulse of submarine volcanism triggers a global episode of oxygen-starved oceans and black-shale deposition near the Cenomanian–Turonian boundary.

title: The granite of Half Dome builds up underground
text: Deep under what will become Yosemite, the Tuolumne Intrusive Suite grows over at least 10 million years, from 95 to 85 million years ago; the Half Dome Granodiorite alone takes almost 4 million years. It was never one great liquid magma chamber but built up in many small increments.

title: _Vegavis_: a duck relative among the dinosaurs
text: A bird from the end of the Cretaceous in Antarctica is a close relative of modern ducks and geese. It shows that lineages of living birds had already split before the asteroid impact, and some survived the mass extinction.

title: _Quetzalcoatlus_: the largest flying animal ever
text: Giant azhdarchid pterosaurs live in latest-Cretaceous Texas, in what is now Big Bend National Park. The giant _Quetzalcoatlus northropi_ is found in river-channel deposits; over 200 specimens of a smaller species, _Q. lawsoni_, come from an old channel lake. One specimen is the youngest pterosaur reported.
notes: Latest Cretaceous per andres2021; t and t_err span the Maastrichtian (ogg2020).

title: Laramide orogeny raises the Rocky Mountains
text: From the Late Cretaceous into the Paleocene, crust is thrust and blocks are pushed up across western North America, building the Rocky Mountain fold-and-thrust belt and Mexico's Sierra Madre Oriental. The deformation lies 700–1500 km inland from the nearest plate boundary, and why remains a puzzle; flat-slab subduction is one proposal.

title: Dinosaurs ate grass
text: Grass fragments in Late Cretaceous dinosaur coprolites from India show grasses had already evolved and diversified before the dinosaurs died out.

title: Chicxulub impact; end of the non-avian dinosaurs
text: A large asteroid strikes the Yucatán; the Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction follows.

art.caption: _Tyrannosaurus rex_, a giant two-legged predator of western North America in the last few million years of the Cretaceous. Large adults are estimated to have weighed roughly 6 to 9 tonnes.

title: Deccan Traps erupt across India
text: Zircon dates show the Deccan flood basalts erupted in four pulses over some 700,000–800,000 years, the first before the end-Cretaceous extinction. How much they contributed alongside the Chicxulub impact is debated.

title: _Purgatorius_: the first primates
text: Teeth from Montana show stem primates appeared within about 100,000–200,000 years after the end-Cretaceous extinction.

art.caption: _Purgatorius_, a small stem primate known from teeth found in Montana.

title: Antrim lavas and the columns of the Giant's Causeway
text: Lava floods Northern Ireland in two main pulses, 62.6 and 59.6 million years ago, part of the volcanism that accompanies the opening of the North Atlantic. In the pause between them, a local flow cools slowly into the famous hexagonal columns of the Giant's Causeway.
notes: ganerod2010: Lower Basalt 62.6 ± 0.3, Tardree rhyolite 61.3 ± 0.3, Upper Basalt 59.6 ± 0.3 Ma. The Causeway Tholeiite's position (after the Tardree rhyolite, before the Upper Basalt) and 'hexagonal columns' are from a GSA Today 2026 summary and general knowledge; the Causeway itself is undated.

title: _Eritherium_: the oldest elephant relative
text: A small, primitive mammal from the late Paleocene of Morocco is the oldest known member of the elephant order (Proboscidea), and among the earliest known members of any modern placental order.

title: _Titanoboa_: the largest snake
text: A boa relative from Colombia's Cerrejón rainforest, 58–60 million years old, about 13 m long and over a tonne. A cold-blooded animal this big needs a mean annual temperature of 30–34 °C.

art.caption: _Titanoboa cerrejonensis_, the largest known snake.

title: Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum
text: Thousands of billions of tonnes of carbon, released in less than 20,000 years, warm the planet by 5–8 °C and acidify the oceans; the whole event lasts about 200,000 years.

title: The first horses shrink as the world heats
text: Early horses get about 30% smaller over the first 130,000 years of the Paleocene–Eocene heat spike, then grow by about 76% as it eases. Body size tracks temperature, probably driven by heat and high carbon dioxide.

title: Saturn's rings may form, younger than most dinosaurs
text: Cassini's measurement of the rings' mass suggests they formed 10–100 million years ago; the rate at which dust pollutes them caps their age at a few hundred million years. Others argue the rings are as old as Saturn.

title: India hits Asia; the Himalaya begins to rise
text: Geological, fossil and paleomagnetic evidence places the start of India's collision with Asia at about 50 million years ago, beginning the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau.

title: Early Eocene Climatic Optimum: the warmest of the Cenozoic
text: Deep-sea isotopes record the warmest sustained climate of the last 66 million years, with no permanent polar ice.

title: Ants become farmers
text: Fungus-growing ants begin cultivating fungi about 50 million years ago in the Neotropics, during the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum. Only four animal groups farm: humans, bark beetles, termites and ants.

title: Europa's present icy surface is laid down
text: Crater counts suggest the surface of Jupiter's moon Europa is only about 30–70 million years old, uncertain by a factor of a few. The ice covers a salty ocean detected by the Galileo spacecraft's magnetometer.

title: _Pakicetus_: whales begin on land
text: Skeletons of _Pakicetus_ from Pakistan show the earliest whales were wolf-sized land animals related to even-toed hoofed mammals.

art.caption: _Pakicetus attocki_, an early Eocene four-legged whale from Pakistan.

title: Drake Passage opens: Pacific water flows into the Southern Ocean
text: Neodymium isotopes in Southern Ocean sediments record shallow Pacific seawater entering the Atlantic sector about 41 million years ago. With the Tasmanian Gateway, this completes a seaway around Antarctica by the late Eocene. Estimates range from 49 to 17 million years ago.

title: _Perucetus_: the heaviest animal ever?
text: A Middle Eocene basilosaurid whale from Peru with extraordinarily dense bones; its skeleton outweighs any known mammal's. First estimates put its body mass above the blue whale's; a reanalysis says it was lighter. Debated.

art.caption: _Perucetus colossus_, reconstructed from vertebrae, ribs and a hip bone.

title: _Basilosaurus_: an early whale at the top of the food chain
text: In the late Eocene seas of what is now Egypt's Wadi Al Hitan, the whale _Basilosaurus isis_ is the apex predator. Its stomach contents hold young whales of another species, _Dorudon_, and large fishes.
notes: Late Eocene per voss2019; t and t_err span the Priabonian (ogg2020). Drawing art/line/basilosaurus.svg (PhyloPic, Tripoli, CC BY) fetched but detached: wide-art layout bug (collision-pages.md).

title: Popigai impact, Siberia
text: Argon dating places the Popigai impact in the late Eocene, near the Eocene–Oligocene boundary, not at the end of the Cretaceous as once suggested.

title: The Alps rise as Adria pushes into Europe
text: The Alpine Tethys ocean between Europe and the Adriatic microplate has been consumed by subduction. From about 35 million years ago the sinking slab rolls back while Adria's rigid core drives into Europe like an indenter, building the Western Alps. Old seafloor slabs are still seen by seismic tomography beneath the Alps and Apennines.
notes: Date from an abstract fragment in web-search results (rollback subduction from 35 Ma coinciding with Western Alpine orogenesis); full abstract not read.

title: Glyptodonts: giant armadillos branch off
text: Ancient DNA from _Doedicurus_ shows that glyptodonts, the huge armoured herbivores whose fossils Darwin collected in South America, belong inside the armadillo family. They split off no earlier than about 35 million years ago and grew spectacularly in size until they died out at the end of the last ice age.

title: Chesapeake Bay impact
text: An impact on the continental shelf of eastern North America creates the buried crater beneath Chesapeake Bay and scatters North American tektites, glass dated to about 34.9 million years ago.

title: Antarctica freezes over
text: Ice sheets grow rapidly on Antarctica in two steps at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary, ending the warm 'greenhouse' world of the early Cenozoic.

title: Kelp forests begin in the cooling North Pacific
text: Fossil kelp holdfasts, the root-like anchors, from western Washington State show kelp growing in the northeastern Pacific from the earliest Oligocene. This fits a North Pacific origin as the world cooled at the Eocene–Oligocene transition; mammals such as desmostylians may have grazed it.
notes: 'Earliest Oligocene' per kiel2024; t ≈ 33.9–32 Ma.

title: The long fall of carbon dioxide begins
text: CO₂ peaks at about 1,500 ppm in the Eocene greenhouse, then falls to about 500 ppm by the Miocene and lower still in the ice-age world. Some two-thirds of the drop comes from oceans holding more alkalinity, probably as weathering outpaced volcanic outgassing. Today's level was last reached about 3 million years ago.

title: _Paraceratherium_: a hornless rhino among the largest land mammals
text: A new species of giant rhinoceros from northwest China, 26.5 million years old, belongs to one of the largest land mammals ever.

art.caption: _Paraceratherium_, a giant hornless rhinoceros.

title: The oldest apes and Old World monkeys, side by side
text: Fossils of an early ape relative and an early Old World monkey relative lie in the same 25.2-million-year-old layer in the East African Rift of Tanzania. Molecular clocks had put the split between apes and Old World monkeys at 25–30 million years ago, but fossils of either were known only from 20 million years.

title: Terror birds: giant flightless predators of South America
text: Phorusrhacids, large flightless birds, are top predators in South America through much of the Cenozoic. Gigantism evolved in one lineage; _Phorusrhacos_, the first of the later giants, was smaller and a better runner than its predecessors, perhaps suited to spreading open country.
notes: Date: Phorusrhacos longissimus is Santacrucian (Early Miocene, ~18–16 Ma); not stated in labarge2024's abstract.

title: Columbia River flood basalts and a warm Miocene
text: Most of the Columbia River flood basalt, Earth's youngest, erupts within about 750,000 years, coinciding with Miocene global warming.

title: Mid-Miocene Climatic Optimum
text: A greenhouse interval of about 2 million years interrupts the long Cenozoic cooling, beginning at about the time the Columbia River basalts erupt.

title: Supernovae blow the Local Bubble around the Sun's neighbourhood
text: A burst of star birth and then supernovae near the bubble's centre begins about 14 million years ago, carving the Local Bubble, the hot, thin cavity the Solar System sits in today. Its expanding shell triggered the formation of nearly all young stars within 200 parsecs.

title: The Solar System passes through the Radcliffe wave
text: Tracing young star clusters back in time shows the Sun crossed this long wave of gas clouds in the Orion region between 18.2 and 11.5 million years ago, closest 14.8–12.4 million years ago, during the Middle Miocene climate transition. A climate link is unproven.

title: Paratethys, the largest lake ever, shrinks
text: Cut off from the ocean, the Paratethys Sea of Eurasia becomes the largest megalake in the geological record. In four droughts it loses up to a third of its water and 70% of its area, exposing up to 1.75 million km² of new land.

title: The central Andes rise rapidly
text: Ancient soils and lake carbonates indicate the central Andean plateau rose by about 2.5 ± 1 km between about 10 and 6 million years ago; the Andes grew in spurts lasting 1–4 million years.

title: Supernova debris falls on Earth
text: Radioactive iron-60, made in supernovae or massive stars within about 100 parsecs (330 light-years), settles onto the ocean floor worldwide.

title: Grasslands spread
text: Carbon isotopes in fossil teeth and soils record a worldwide expansion of C4 grasses between about 8 and 6 million years ago, creating savannahs.

title: The Sahara becomes a desert
text: Wind-blown dune sands in Chad record desert conditions 7 million years ago, and climate models tie the drying to the shrinking of the Tethys Sea in the Late Miocene. Many researchers instead date the Sahara to 2–3 million years ago; debated.

title: _Sahelanthropus_: the oldest possible hominin
text: A skull from Chad, about 6–7 million years old, may be the earliest member of the human lineage after its split from chimpanzees.

title: The Mediterranean dries out
text: Cut off from the Atlantic, the Mediterranean largely evaporates, leaving salt layers more than a kilometre thick on its floor.

title: _Ardipithecus kadabba_
text: Fossils from Ethiopia's Middle Awash, 5.2–5.8 million years old, are among the oldest hominins.

title: Giordano Bruno, one of the Moon's youngest large craters, forms
text: Small craters on the ejecta of this 22 km crater give an age of 1 to 10 million years, ruling out the idea that it formed in 1178 AD when medieval monks reported a flash on the Moon.

title: The Grand Canyon is carved
text: The Colorado River links older canyon segments, some 70–50 and 25–15 million years old, and cuts the Grand Canyon from 5–6 million years ago.

title: The Zanclean flood refills the Mediterranean
text: The Atlantic breaks through at Gibraltar; most of the refilling may have taken from a few months to two years, with peak flows far greater than any river today.

title: Laetoli: footprints of upright walkers
text: Trails of footprints pressed into wet volcanic ash at Laetoli, Tanzania, show hominins walking upright on two feet some 3.6–3.7 million years ago.

title: Megalodon, the giant shark, dies out
text: The youngest reliable fossils of _Otodus megalodon_, last of the giant 'megatoothed' shark lineage that began in the Paleocene, are early Pliocene; later teeth are reworked from older rocks. It vanishes about 3.6 million years ago, so it is not still lurking in the deep.

title: The oldest stone tools: Lomekwi
text: Stone flakes and cores from Lomekwi 3, West Turkana, Kenya, are 3.3 million years old, 700,000 years older than the Oldowan tools long thought the earliest.

title: Lucy
text: The partial skeleton of _Australopithecus afarensis_ found at Hadar, Ethiopia, nicknamed Lucy, is dated by argon in volcanic crystals to 3.18 million years; the 'First Family' fossils nearby to 3.20 million.

art.caption: _Australopithecus afarensis_, Lucy's species.

title: The Isthmus of Panama closes
text: A land bridge joins North and South America about 2.8 million years ago, separating the Pacific from the Caribbean and letting animals cross between the continents.

title: Ice sheets spread across the Northern Hemisphere
text: After millions of years of slow cooling, large ice sheets begin to grow on North America and Eurasia, one of the most dramatic climate shifts on record. A warmer late summer in the stratified subarctic Pacific may have supplied the moisture that fell as snow over northern North America.

title: Supernova debris falls on Earth again
text: A second, global influx of interstellar iron-60 reaches the seafloor, evidence of one or more nearby supernovae.

title: Yellowstone's first and largest caldera eruption
text: The Huckleberry Ridge Tuff erupts from the Yellowstone hotspot, the earliest and largest of its caldera-forming eruptions. Zircon crystals show that one part of the magma body evolved in only about 10,000 years before it blew.

title: Fire in a cave: Wonderwerk
text: Burned bone and ashed plants in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, about 1 million years old, are the earliest secure evidence of fire in an archaeological site.

title: Mid-Pleistocene Transition: ice ages lengthen to 100,000 years
text: Between 1.25 million and 700,000 years ago, without any change in Earth's orbit, ice ages switch from a 41,000-year rhythm to longer, deeper cycles of about 100,000 years, and ice volume grows by about 50 m of sea level. One idea: glaciers scraped off the soil to bare bedrock, where thicker ice sheets could grip.

title: Human ancestors nearly die out
text: Modern genomes suggest our ancestors fell to about 1,280 breeding individuals between about 930,000 and 813,000 years ago, a bottleneck lasting some 117,000 years that matches a gap in the fossil record. Debated.

art.caption: Schematic: only the bottleneck's size and timing are data, about 1,280 breeding individuals for 117,000 years.

title: Last full reversal of Earth's magnetic field
text: After excursions at 795,000 and 784,000 years ago, the field makes its final flip to today's polarity, the Brunhes–Matuyama reversal, 773,000 years ago.

title: Small hominins on Flores
text: A jaw and teeth from Mata Menge on Flores, Indonesia, about 700,000 years old, come from small-jawed relatives of _Homo floresiensis_, the 'hobbit'. Whether it shrank from _Homo erectus_ on the island (island dwarfism) is debated.

art.caption: _Homo floresiensis_, known from Liang Bua cave on Flores.

title: The Great Barrier Reef starts to grow
text: Deep cores show that reef growth on Australia's outer barrier began only about 600,000 years ago, after the last full magnetic reversal. It may have been triggered by the large 100,000-year swings of sea level that came with the long ice-age cycles; stacked reef layers separated by old land surfaces record it dying back and regrowing as the sea fell and rose.

title: Earliest _Homo sapiens_: Jebel Irhoud
text: Fossils from Morocco dated to about 315,000 years ago push the origin of our species back by some 100,000 years.

title: Earth's orbit paces the ice ages
text: Deep-sea sediments of the last 450,000 years show climate swinging at periods of 23,000, 42,000 and about 100,000 years, matching wobbles in Earth's axis and orbit: the Milankovitch cycles.

title: Toba supereruption, Sumatra
text: The largest volcanic eruption on land in the Quaternary; its ash and sulfate reach both hemispheres. Its effect on climate and on people is debated: in South Africa, humans thrived through it.

title: Oldest known narrative cave art
text: A painted scene of human-like figures with a wild pig in a Sulawesi cave, Indonesia, is at least 51,200 years old.

title: Meteor Crater, Arizona, is blasted out
text: Cosmogenic isotopes in boulders thrown out by the impact date Meteor Crater (Barringer Crater) to about 49,000–50,000 years ago.

title: Laschamps excursion: the field briefly flips
text: Earth's field weakens and briefly reverses about 41,000 years ago; New Zealand kauri tree rings record a surge of radiocarbon as cosmic rays increase. Its proposed role in a global environmental crisis is debated.

title: Ice Age megafauna disappear
text: Mammoths, giant ground sloths and many other large animals vanish from most continents. Humans and climate change both played a part; their relative roles are debated.

title: Last Glacial Maximum
text: Nearly all ice sheets reach their greatest extent of the last ice age, and sea level stands about 130 m lower than today.

title: The great melt begins
text: Rising northern summer sunshine starts to melt the Northern Hemisphere ice sheets 19,000–20,000 years ago, and sea level begins an abrupt rise. West Antarctica follows 14,000–15,000 years ago, probably the main source of a sudden jump in sea level about 14,500 years ago.

title: Lake Victoria dries up, then fills with new fish species
text: Lake Victoria dried out completely before 12,400 radiocarbon years ago, yet today it holds more than 300 endemic cichlid species: one of the fastest bursts of speciation known.

art.caption: A cichlid fish. Lake Victoria's hundreds of endemic species evolved since the lake refilled.

title: Niagara Falls nearly stalls as the upper lakes drain elsewhere
text: From about 10,500 to 5,500 years ago the water of the upper Great Lakes bypasses Lake Erie, flowing out through North Bay to the Ottawa River. Starved of flow, Niagara Falls creeps very slowly around the narrow bend at Niagara Glen; it speeds up again once the water returns.
notes: Ages are radiocarbon years before 1950 (yr B.P.) as given; uncalibrated.

title: The last mammoths: dwarfs on Wrangel Island
text: Teeth of dwarf woolly mammoths on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean date to 7,000–4,000 years ago, long after mammoths vanished elsewhere.

art.caption: Woolly mammoth, _Mammuthus primigenius_. The Wrangel Island population shrank in body size.

title: Tunguska explosion flattens a Siberian forest
text: On 30 June 1908 a stony asteroid tens of metres across disintegrates 5–10 km above Siberia, flattening over 2,000 km² of forest. No crater was found; nearby Lake Cheko has been proposed as one (debated).
notes: t assumes present = 2026; settle the present-year convention in session 15 (page 914 design).

title: Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 crashes into Jupiter
text: Fragments of a comet that had broken apart near Jupiter strike the planet on 16–22 July 1994. The Hubble Space Telescope images the plumes and the dark impact sites in Jupiter's atmosphere.
notes: t assumes present = 2026; settle the present-year convention in session 15 (page 914 design).

title: Chelyabinsk airburst over Russia
text: On 15 February 2013 an asteroid about 20 m across explodes over Chelyabinsk with an energy of roughly 500 kilotons, the largest impact on Earth since 1908, damaging buildings across the region.
notes: t assumes present = 2026; settle the present-year convention in session 15 (page 914 design).
